title: Nemetschek & Novatr Sign MoU to Support Viksit Bharat 2047
summary: Nemetschek and Novatr sign an MoU to advance AEC education, digital skills, and innovation in India, supporting the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
body_text: In light of recognising this gap and opportunity, Novatr and Nemetschek India have signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to help strengthen and build India's Architecture, Engineering and Construction (AEC) talent ecosystem. Together, the two organisations aim to make globally recognised technologies, industry-relevant learning and digital capabilities more accessible to students, professionals, enterprises and academic institutions across the country. Through this collaboration, Novatr learners will gain access to Nemetschek's leading technology portfolio, including Graphisoft Archicad, Allplan, Bluebeam, Solibri and Vectorworks. These technologies will be integrated into Novatr's project-based, cohort-driven programmes, alongside dedicated certification pathways that enable learners to build practical, job-ready skills through real-world projects and industry-standard digital workflows. Commenting on the partnership, Harkunwar Singh, Co-founder & CEO, Novatr, said that "The future of the AEC industry depends on professionals who are proficient in digital design, collaboration and construction technologies. By partnering with Nemetschek India, we are enabling learners to master globally used BIM platforms while working on real-world industry scenarios. This collaboration strengthens our mission of making India's AEC workforce globally competitive and helping employers access talent that is productive from day one." The partnership further strengthens Nemetschek India and Novatr’s commitment to building higher standards of education in the country. In recent years, Nemetschek India has partnered with leading institutions such as IIT Madras, VJTI, the School of Planning and Architecture (SPA), and KIIT, while also expanding its Global Capability Centre in India. Now, Novatr is joining the esteemed lineup. This new collaboration is designed to equip talent for the future of digital construction. Speaking on the collaboration, Alok Sharma, Managing Director and Vice President, Nemetschek India, said: "India is entering a defining decade for infrastructure and urban development, where digital technologies and AI will determine how efficiently we design, build and operate our built environment. While BIM adoption is accelerating rapidly, the availability of industry-ready digital talent remains one of the sector's biggest challenges. Our partnership with Novatr reflects Nemetschek's long-term commitment to developing future-ready professionals by giving them access to globally recognised BIM and AI-driven technologies, practical project experience and internationally relevant digital workflows. Together, we aim to build a stronger, globally competitive talent pipeline, one that not only supports India's transition towards smarter, more sustainable and technology-driven construction, but is also skilled enough to cater to global design and engineering needs."

title: Two Speed Shops Live and Breathe American Muscle… with an English Twist
summary: If you’re after a lot of horsepower from a classic Chevy, Ford, or Chrysler race engine, you might think the only place to go is the United States. After all, these engines have been extensively developed over the years for all sorts of racing in the U.S., from sports and formula cars to dragsters and […]
body_text: If you’re after a lot of horsepower from a classic Chevy, Ford, or Chrysler race engine, you might think the only place to go is the United States. After all, these engines have been extensively developed over the years for all sorts of racing in the U.S., from sports and formula cars to dragsters and sedans, and everything in between. However, deep in the British countryside, we visited two companies making American horsepower for drag and circuit racing: Mathwall and I.C.E. Automotive Engines. It turns out that racers in the U.K. and Europe often take advantage of the expertise in building these engines in England, of all places. That’s for two main reasons. One: because U.K.-based companies can provide on-site service. And two: because there are very specific classes and rules for drag and circuit racing in Europe. For example, the governing body of world motorsport, the FIA, has strict rules for pre-1966 race cars like Shelby Cobras and Ford GT40s. All of this is detailed in Appendix K, which is the FIA’s rulebook for historic road-course and rally racing. In the U.S., you can run roller rockers and all sorts of tweaks that would get you thrown out of a sports car or sedan race featuring Cobras and Mustangs in Europe. Of course, everyone who goes racing wants to get as much power and torque from a full-race V-8 as they can, but tailoring these engines to Appendix K rules is a specialized art. Among the engines at Mathwall awaiting attention is this big-block twin-turbo Ford engine for a customer in Poland. Mark Gillies It’s the same with dragsters. Positioned below what people regard as the pinnacle of drag racing—Top Fuel dragsters and Funny Cars—there are classes specific to European drag racing. And as with all forms of vintage motorsports, the Brits have become very adept at building engines for so-called nostalgia drags. Mathwall Mathwall’s Ford 289 engine is basically all-new, save for the timing cover. Mark Gillies Based in rural Surrey, south of London, Mathwall began business in 1967. It was formed by Stuart Mathieson and Peter Wallace, who had worked at Alan Mann Racing on their successful European Ford racing programs, with cars like the GT40 and Mustang. Their first job was to prepare a customer Ford Falcon for sedan racing and, while they branched out with automakers such as Mazda and BMW, they continually built Ford and Chevrolet engines for road and race applications. Mathwall and Purple Sector owner Mark Mathieson stands by a photo that shows his Ford Mustang on the front row of the Ken Miles Trophy at the 2024 Goodwood Members’ Meeting. Mark Gillies The company has expanded somewhat since Stuart Mathieson’s son, Mark, took over the business in 2007. As well as building engines, Mathwall Technologies developed into an engineering services business that has been rebranded as Purple Sector, an engineering-led and data-driven consultancy. This builds on the work that Mark Mathieson did as an engineer on F1 powerplants at Ilmor/Mercedes-Benz and during the COVID pandemic, when he spearheaded rush production of ICU ventilators for the National Health Service. While it’s a smaller part of the business these days, Mathwall still produces Ford and Chevy V-8 engines for historic racing, used in cars like Ford GT40s, Ford Mustangs, Shelby Cobras, and Bizzarrini 5300GTs. Specifically, these engines are built to the FIA’s Appendix K rules, and they are bespoke units. Development engineer Liam Draper studies computer drawings of a small-block Chevy crankshaft that sits on the bench in front of him. Mark Gillies “We’re the only ones, to my knowledge, that design our own cam profiles, design our own valvetrain, cranks, rods, pistons,” Mark Mathieson tells us. “Obviously, we put all the internals together with a replacement block and cylinder heads. It’s a new engine, and we are in control of the parts that make the engine breathe and give it the torque and power characteristics that we want to have. Piston and connecting rod for a Ford 289 engine. Made by U.K. manufacturers to Mathwall’s specifications. Mark Gillies “Every engine gets built with known parts from approved suppliers, inspected to a process. Blueprinted build, all recorded. Goes on the dyno, goes through a very arduous and thorough break-in and test cycle. When it’s been through that, it gets its final inspection, then it comes off, gets a leak-down check, borescope, oil samples taken. Once it has gone through all of that, if it has a problem when it first goes in the car, it’s likely to be an installation issue, because we know the engine’s good to go at that point.” Ford 289 engine in build, showing fitted pistons, crank, and rods. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mathwall builds for the premium end of the market, Mathieson points out: “It’s a more discerning customer who appreciates some of what I just described and will pay for it. Because of the way the business is set up, I don’t need to be chasing 50 to 100 engines every year. I’m quite happy if we do a number of 20, maybe 30 a year.” These are essentially new engines; Mathieson feels that’s the only way you can guarantee reliability. Development engineer Liam Draper expands on this as he shows me around the spotless engine build facility and the engine dynamometer. The company uses modern tools such as a FaroArm, CAD software, and 3D printing to rapid prototype parts like cylinder head ports and test them on a flow bench. In the past, they would have had to work away on a grinding bench for hours to achieve the same result. Among the tools employees like Draper use is this FaroArm: a portable co-ordinate measuring machine that can be used to reverse-engineer components using CAD modeling. Mark Gillies In period, he says a Ford 289 race engine made around 370 horsepower. These days, Draper says a Mathwall 289 for a GT40 or Cobra makes in the 440-450-hp region, but that drivability is more important than outright power. “We know we can get the horsepower out of these engines,” he says. “But then you end up with an engine that a pro might be able to drive around a track like Goodwood very quickly, but an owner might struggle with it. So actually, getting the torque curve right is way more important. Also, we go to a whole range of tracks that are very different. Getting a nice drivable package for everyone, everywhere is key, really. “Mark [Matheison] spent a lot of time in Formula 1 at Ilmor/Mercedes, and his big thing was valves, valve springs, camshafts, controlling that environment, so he’s very clued up and knows all about camshaft design. There are natural inefficiencies with a Ford 289 engine, but we’re running more valve lift for longer thanks to the cam design.” When it comes to Appendix K regulations, Draper outlines key differences between them and the freedom an engine builder would have in American vintage racing. “The main difference that you get from one of our engines and an American equivalent is normally around the valvetrain. We have to run solid tappets here, non-roller rockers, and a cast-iron camshaft. In America, you find that they’re running steel camshafts, roller lifters, and roller rockers. It just means you can put in a lot more lift and take the stress off the camshaft. We are governed by a 7000-rpm limit, as well. Ford 289 engine uses a new block: Mathwall maintains that the only way to guarantee reliability is to build engines from new components. Mark Gillies “We’re allowed to run an MSD ignition controller, which is great because it keeps the playing field level: they are scrutineered for each race and for rev limit. The quality of points ignition just isn’t there anymore. You know with the MSD, you can sit at 7000 all day and the ignition isn’t going to start floating.” Under Appendix K, porting is free and the valve size is set, but they also measure the ports to ensure no one is raising them. Draper points out that every time Mathwall builds an engine, it gets Motorsport U.K.—which governs racing in Britain—to seal the engines on site and check the capacity, valve sizes, and bore and stroke. FIA-spec Ford 289 sedan engine on Mathwall’s in-house engine dyno: This allows the company to tune the engine with representative exhaust systems. Mark Gillies The dyno has been designed and built in-house. It’s rated up to 628 hp, but Draper says that what sets it apart is its ability to go up to 10,000 rpm and around 1325 pound-feet of torque. With 200 channels of data logging, Mathwall has the ability to do all its own development. Mathwall also offers valuable customer service. The dyno, for instance, allows the company to run different exhaust systems—be they Cobra, Mustang, or GT40, for example—which enables engineers to get the fuelling right for the engine before it goes into the car. And then, they always try to look at the actual car and make sure the install is done properly so there are no issues with how the engine runs. The dyno was designed and built in-house and allows Mathwall to log 200 channels of data if needed. It can handle more than 670 horsepower and 1300 pound-feet of torque. Mark Gillies Mathieson says that the company actually has a pool of engines ready so that it can simply adapt an engine to the specific vehicle application and not have to scramble with rebuilding a customer’s engine, which has often returned because it has reached its designated number of running hours. “You just need to be ahead of the game,” he says. “The buffer stop takes the stress out of the business.” Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies I.C.E. Automotive Engines Nick Davies is one of the two owners of I.C.E. Automotive Racing Engines, along with Rob Loaring. Mark Gillies Like Mathwall, I.C.E. Automotive Engines has been around a while. Rob Loaring founded the company in 1988 in Southend, east of London. In 1998, he was joined by Neil Davies, a one-time bond trader who “decided it would be a good idea to give up work” and go into partnership with the man who built the engines for his cars. Initially, they worked out of Loaring’s Southend premises, before moving to the Silverstone Technology Park in the English Midlands in around 2005. Today, though, Loaring operates in a shop near Silverstone and Davies operates near Banbury, around 30 miles away. “Rob has got the big machines,” says Davies: “the dyno and the flow bench, the big honing machine.” The “big machines” live at the shop of Davies’ business partner, Rob Loaring. Davies says they both need to do a lot of machine work, hence this milling machine. Mark Gillies Davies used to race this Austin Bantam AA/FA dragster called “Havoc:” It has run 5.98 seconds at 237 mph and won its class at the California Hot Rod Reunion in 2017. Mark Gillies For a while, I.C.E. built engines for circuit racing: “predominantly historic American stuff,” says Davies. They have dialed back on the circuit racing engines and, Davies says, “These days, it’s predominantly drags. We’re building more custom stuff, application-specific for specific class racing. And it’s still across the board, but not so many small-blocks: The drags tend to use bigger capacity engines because there’s no penalty for using them. So, we’re back on big Chevrolets, big Chryslers. We also have the odd Ford.” When I visited Davies’ shop in the summer, he was working on a number of engines but stressed that the off-season is when they do most of their builds. “Most of the engines that we build will need servicing every, let’s say, couple of years. A lot of them use aluminum rods, a roller valvetrain, fairly high spring pressures. So, things need looking at and servicing on a fairly regular basis.” When we visited, Davies was in the process of finishing a 600-cubic-inch big-block Chevy in a 2004 Grand Am for his daughter to race. Mark Gillies In the shop, he showed me several engines. First up was a 600-cubic-inch naturally aspirated Chevy, fitted into a 2004 Pontiac Grand Am that runs in a class called SuperGas. This one makes 920 horsepower and will be driven by Davies’ 16-year-old daughter. “Quite terrifying, really,” he says. Then there was a big-block twin-turbo Ford engine with a broken rod that was in for a rebuild; a 468-cubic-inch big-block Chevy for a street rod; and two Chrysler blocks, one for a 450-cubic-inch supercharged nitro Nostalgia Funny Car and the other for a twin-turbo alcohol Pro-Modified car. Davies estimates that the blown nitro Hemi in “Havoc” makes “3200 hp based on its weight and how fast it has gone.” Mark Gillies The engine in Davies’ own outrageous Fiat Topolino AA/Fuel Altered is a 417 cubic-inch Hemi, with an original type of magnesium supercharger and intake manifold, running on nitro-methane. Davies reckons it makes around 2000 hp, but he also has an Austin Bantam that won the California Hotrod Reunion in 2017. That one makes around 3000 hp, Davies says, based on the car’s weight and a 5.98 quarter-mile at 240 mph. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Another blown Hemi sits up front in Davies’ Fiat Topolino “No Quarter.” He reckons the engine makes “around 2000 horsepower.” Mark Gillies Why the estimates? “We can’t actually measure the power,” Davies says. “Our dyno is pegged at 1000 pound-feet of torque. We use the dyno to break rings in and make sure they don’t leak, but can’t really tune the engine because of the limitations of the dyno. However, we run data loggers and record everything on them from boost to clutch speed. I can’t do anything without a logger.” I.C.E builds engines for all forms of drag racing, save for the “Top Fuel Funny Car stuff,” he says. “The ‘ nostalgia scene ‘ seems to be growing fairly well over here, and within that there are several different classes that we get involved with. Over here, Street Eliminator for streetable cars running on radial tires is in a growth phase. Other than no wheelie bars, a governed tire, and running on some kind of pump gas, it’s kind of free. We build for two or three of the fastest guys that run big-inch turbos. Piston on a big-block 468-cubic-inch Chevy street rod engine. Mark Gillies “We’ve got a customer who’s won five or six championships with, would you believe, a 1956 Chevy with a 660-cubic-inch twin-turbo engine on E85. It has run 215, and to make that kind of speed, it must produce around 2000 hp. On a radial tire, and he can drive it around the streets. Part of the qualifying at every meeting at which these cars run is they have to go out on the public roads and do a 30-mile cruise. It’s mandatory to have MoTs.” (An MoT is the U.K.’s mandatory test of vehicle roadworthiness.) Turbos are now competing with classical supercharging on all but the top classes, Davies says. “There’s a class that runs here and, in the U.S., called Pro Modified. In Europe, you can only run three types of engines: huge-inch nitrous engines, which are up to now 960 cubic inches; the second option is supercharged; and the third option is turbocharged. And for the last two or three years, the turbochargers, much as they’ve been handcuffed, have come out on top in the FIA championship. “We chose the turbo route. The turbos are more complicated, but you absolutely can make more horsepower with them. The other nice thing is the operating RPM is significantly lower than the supercharger combination. We decided at our age, we didn’t want to do the work in the pits. You’ll see people with supercharged cars breaking stuff on a very regular basis. Well, we’d rather be lighting a barbecue while they’re fixing their engine. Davies and Loaring are both members of the British Drag Racing Hall of Fame. As well as racing “Havoc,” Davies has campaigned this twin-turbo Pro Modified Firebird. Mark Gillies “I guess that the popular or common understanding is that the supercharged engines at the drags go fastest, because all the nitro classes are supercharged. Below that, I think the clever people would say it’s easier to make a huge amount of horsepower reliably from turbochargers than it is from superchargers. The parasitic loss from a supercharger is extraordinary. With the turbochargers, it’s not free horsepower because there’s a restriction on the exhaust side of things, but it’s nothing like as significant as the supercharger. We’ve built a lot of turbo stuff, and we’re quite recognized as we can tune them, as well, on the various engine management programs. I’m not afraid of a laptop.” Davies says that the raw components come from the U.S., but that I.C.E. “can’t get exactly what we want. We can’t get heads with the right size intake runners, for instance. So, we get into a fair amount of machining. We don’t just assemble components. We’ll look into the corners and try to optimize the components we put together.” Davies shares that, since COVID and the continuing consolidation of the American speed industry, lead times have become stretched, bigger companies are less interested in servicing small clients, and some of the institutional knowledge has gone. Close-up of welded aluminum intake for the twin-turbo big-block Ford engine. Mark Gillies U.K. customers could go to a U.S. engine specialist and ship an engine over, but Davies says there are some advantages with going to I.C.E. “I guess the first one is that people rely on you for support on the ground. How good an experience do you get from someone who is remote and 5000 miles away? It is very easy not to prioritize someone who isn’t standing in front of you. “Here you get honest horsepower. We have a notoriously stingy dyno. A lot of our engines win races. We don’t try to sell on dyno numbers. Rob and I decided years ago we didn’t want to give any happy numbers just to please our customers. We have had customers bring engines to us that show that the horsepower numbers that some people advertise just aren’t there. Davies at work on the big-block Chevy engine. Most of the parts come from the U.S., but Davies says he and Loaring do “a fair amount of machining” to optimize components. Mark Gillies “We might be a bit more expensive than a U.S. engine builder who builds a comparable engine—maybe because they have better buying power than us—but I would argue you don’t get exactly the same engine, and you absolutely don’t get the same support. We might not be able to track every run an engine makes, but once we deliver, we will go to the drag strip for the first or second time a customer runs it just to make sure everything is OK. We are not just engine builders; we’re in the service industry.” Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies The post Two Speed Shops Live and Breathe American Muscle… with an English Twist appeared first on Hagerty Media .

body_text: View all news Neighborhood Intelligence Board Initiates Immediate Process to Unlock Value of Blockchain and Digital Assets 08/17/2026 Download (opens in new window) PDF 105 KB Process includes tZERO, GrainChain and Medici Ventures; Company to pursue and respond to paths already brought forward and other opportunities that may be available NASHVILLE, Tenn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Neighborhood Intelligence, Inc. (Nasdaq: NXH) (“Neighborhood Intelligence” or the “Company”) today announced that its Board of Directors has determined that now is the time to take action to unlock the value of the Company’s strategic investments in tZERO, GrainChain, and Medici Ventures. The Company believes these assets represent significant value that is severely underappreciated within Neighborhood Intelligence today. The businesses have progressed, their opportunities have expanded, and the Company is seeing interest from parties that recognize the strategic value of what it owns. Neighborhood Intelligence intends to unlock that value and provide its shareholders access to it. The Board has authorized an immediate process to evaluate and pursue value-creation alternatives for the Company’s strategic investments, including paths already presented to the Company, and additional alternatives that may be available. The Company is forming a special committee of independent directors and engaging an investment banking firm to help the Board identify, evaluate and execute the best available alternatives. The process is underway, and the Company expects actionable choices in short order. The announcement comes as the Company begins trading as Neighborhood Intelligence on Nasdaq. “We believe these assets are severely underappreciated, and the time to act is now,” said Marcus Lemonis, Executive Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Neighborhood Intelligence. “Our strategy has not changed. What may change is the address of our ownership—not our belief in the opportunity. We believe a different structure may provide greater visibility, allow the market to more appropriately value these assets and, most importantly, provide our shareholders access to that value while preserving our ability to participate in their future.” Why Now These businesses have progressed from earlier-stage investments into more mature companies with broader capabilities and opportunities. At the same time, the environment surrounding tokenization, digital ownership, real-world assets and related infrastructure has evolved considerably. Neighborhood Intelligence is already engaged in discussions with parties that see strategic value in the Company’ assets, including opportunities to combine with exiting capabilities or enhance Neighborhood Intelligence’s growth potential. Those discussions reinforce the Company’s belief that multiple credible paths are available. Alternatives may include strategic investments, partnerships or combinations, asset contributions, monetizations, public-market transactions, retained ownership through different structures, distributions to shareholders or other alternatives. Different assets may follow different paths. The Strategy Has Not Changed Neighborhood Intelligence continues to see significant opportunities at the intersection of title, real estate, tokenization, digital ownership, transaction infrastructure and liquidity. Every real-estate transaction requires ownership to be established, transferred and recorded. The Company believes there are opportunities to modernize that process and connect traditional ownership infrastructure with technologies that can influence how real-world assets are financed, recorded, transferred and made liquid. Neighborhood Intelligence believes tZERO and other capabilities represented within the portfolio can play an important role as real-world assets increasingly intersect with regulated digital markets. A different ownership structure could provide greater visibility and more appropriate market valuation while allowing Neighborhood Intelligence to maintain meaningful economic participation and provide its shareholders access to that value. Unlocking an asset does not require abandoning it. A strategic combination, contribution into another public company or other structure could establish independent market visibility and valuation while preserving economic participation and strategic relationships. The Company believes combining complementary assets and capabilities may create significantly more value than they can create independently. Neighborhood Intelligence also understands the structure through which certain investments are held. Pelion Venture Partners manages Medici Ventures and retains its contractual rights and economics. Any alternative involving assets held through Medici will be evaluated and structured in light of that relationship. Process Underway Neighborhood Intelligence is pursuing opportunities, responding to interest and engaging with the companies in which it holds these investments about paths available to create value. The special committee and the Company’s financial adviser will evaluate the paths already brought forward, pursue other paths that may be available and help the Company move quickly. Neighborhood Intelligence expects actionable choices in short order. About Neighborhood Intelligence Bed Bath & Beyond, Inc. (Nasdaq: NXH), soon to become Neighborhood Intelligence and trading on Nasdaq under ticker NXH starting today, is a data and technology company focused on simplifying homeownership and making it more affordable. Through three interconnected pillars—Omni-Channel Retail, Home Services, and Home Ownership—the company uses proprietary data, technology, and neighborhood-level intelligence to connect products, services, financing, and expertise into a seamless customer experience. The company's portfolio includes Bed Bath & Beyond, Overstock, buybuy BABY, Kirkland's, The Container Store, Elfa, Closet Works, and, upon completion of the merger, Lumber Liquidators, Cabinets To Go, as well as an expanding portfolio of Home Services and Home Ownership businesses. Together, these businesses help customers create, improve, maintain, protect, finance, and transition their homes while serving them throughout the homeownership journey. Connecting every part of the business is Neighborhood Intelligence, the company's intelligence layer. It leverages proprietary data, artificial intelligence, modern technology, blockchain, tokenization, and innovative financial infrastructure to improve decision-making, reduce friction, enhance operational efficiency, and deliver a more connected customer experience. By combining neighborhood-level intelligence with trusted brands and integrated capabilities, the company helps customers make more informed decisions while lowering the overall cost and complexity of homeownership. The company is committed to innovation, disciplined execution, and making homeownership simpler and more affordable while creating long-term value for its customers, employees, partners, and shareholders. Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements This communication contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Such forward-looking statements include all statements other than statements of historical fact, including but not limited to statements regarding plans and strategies for the Company; planned acquisitions; our industry, business strategy, plans, goals and expectations concerning our market position, future operations and other financial and operating information and the success and timing of any of the foregoing. Forward-looking statements are neither promises nor guarantees, but involve known and unknown risks, uncertainties and other important factors that may cause our actual results, performance or achievements to be materially different from any future results, performance or achievements expressed or implied by the forward-looking statements, including, but not limited to: uncertainties of the consummation of the proposed transaction with Fathom Holdings Inc.; and other important factors discussed under the caption “Risk Factors” in the Company’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025 and Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended June 30, 2026, as such factors may be updated from time to time in the Company’s subsequent filings with the SEC. Strategic Investments Information and Economic Interests Neighborhood Intelligence’s economic interests in these businesses exist both directly and through its approximately 99% ownership of the limited-partner economics of Medici Ventures. tZERO represents the Company’s largest strategic blockchain investment. Based on current fully diluted capitalization information available to the Company, Neighborhood Intelligence directly owns approximately 22.6% of tZERO on a fully diluted, as-converted basis. Medici Ventures owns an additional approximately 16.1%. On a simple gross look-through basis, before giving effect to the economics of the Medici partnership, the Company’s direct ownership together with its economic exposure through Medici represents approximately 38.7% of tZERO. Neighborhood Intelligence believes this represents the largest economic ownership position in the company. tZERO has built regulated infrastructure connecting traditional financial markets with the emerging tokenized economy. Its capabilities span issuance and tokenization, trading, custody, settlement and transfer-agent services and can be integrated into the platforms of banks, broker-dealers, asset managers, fintech companies and other institutions. Neighborhood Intelligence believes this infrastructure can become increasingly important as securities, private-market investments and real-world assets move toward digital ownership and more efficient trading and settlement. As its largest economic owner, Neighborhood Intelligence believes this is an appropriate time for tZERO to evaluate every opportunity available to expand its reach, accelerate its growth and establish greater visibility into the value of what it has built. GrainChain provides technology connecting participants across supply chains, improving visibility, traceability and the movement of goods, data and payments. Its business has expanded beyond its initial focus on agriculture and has broader potential across physical supply chains and real-world commerce. Neighborhood Intelligence’s economic exposure exists both directly through convertible notes, including accrued interest, and indirectly through Medici Ventures. Neighborhood Intelligence also owns approximately 99% of the limited-partner economics of Medici Ventures, providing economic exposure to its broader investment portfolio, subject to Pelion Venture Partners’ contractual rights and economics. The Company will validate the current capitalization, accrued interest and economics of each investment before final publication of its ownership information. title: 2027 Ford Explorer Pricing, Specs, and Release Date
summary: The 2027 Ford Explorer debuts an all-new Sinister Package for the performance Explorer ST model. It comes with unique exterior styling and an invitation to a new Ford driving experience.
body_text: Ford bills the 2027 Explorer ST Sinister Package as a tribute to the type of aftermarket modifications consumers have been making since the Blue Oval introduced the performance-oriented ST model for its midsize three-row SUV in 2020. It opts for black exterior accents to give the Explorer ST a, well, sinister look to go with its performance. 2027 Ford Explorer Pricing, Specs, and Release Date What’s New for the 2027 Ford Explorer Design Powertrain Interior Technology Safety Pricing and Release Date Further Research What’s New for the 2027 Ford Explorer The Explorer ST Sinister Package is new for 2027 as part of what will certainly be a carry-over ST trim level. This is the first 2027 Explorer to be announced, but expect the rest of the line to return. It’s essentially a black-out package for the range-topping, performance-tuned Explorer ST. In addition to the visual features it brings, it includes an invitation to the Explorer ST Experience, a one-day driving school set to launch this fall and tour the country. Design Three-row SUVs are family-oriented and traditionally rather frumpy. With its rear-wheel-drive (RWD) platform, the Explorer takes on a sporty appearance. However, it balances that with some of the machismo of today’s large SUVs. Up front, it has a high-set, large, black grille flanked by eye-slit LED headlights and sharply defined lower air intakes. The body takes on a bit of a rake to make it look predatory, and the profile is highlighted by a forward-angled rear pillar and a high beltline. The ST Sinister Package features include dark-accented Sinister ST badges, amber daytime running lights (DRLs), and large gloss-black 21-inch wheels instead of the ST’s standard Magnetite (dark gray) wheels. Inside, the ST features some sporty elements, including the flat-bottomed steering wheel, red contrast stitching, and synthetic suede and synthetic leather upholstery. Powertrain Like any ST model, the ST Sinister Package comes standard with a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V6. It makes 400 horsepower in its standard tune, but that drops to 385 hp for the states that follow California emissions rules. Torque sits at 415 pound-feet no matter the hp. This special version of the Explorer will have the same 10-speed automatic and standard RWD as the 2026 Explorer ST. Special ST features include six drive modes, a quad-tipped exhaust, a sport-tuned suspension, 21-inch alloy wheels, and larger performance brakes with red calipers. Interior Expect the Explorer ST Sinister Package to be equipped like the 2026 Explorer ST, but with a few tweaks outlined above. That means it should come with synthetic leather and synthetic suede upholstery, a 10-way power-adjustable driver’s seat, a six-way power front passenger seat, heated and ventilated front seats, a heated steering wheel, heated second-row captain’s chairs, a power-folding third row, tri-zone automatic climate control, and ambient lighting. A panoramic fixed glass roof is optional. Cargo space for the 2026 Explorer is 16.3 cubic feet behind the third row, 46 cubic feet behind the second row with the third row folded, and 85.8 cubic feet behind the first row with the rear two rows folded down. Technology Ford outfits the 2026 Explorer ST with a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster, a 13.2-inch infotainment touchscreen, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, a satellite radio trial, a 5G Wi-Fi hotspot, and a 10-speaker B&O audio system. The infotainment system offers Google Maps, the Google Play store, and a Google Assistant. The hotspot is part of a year of the Ford Connectivity Package, which also offers video conferencing, a web browser, and audio and video streaming. It includes forward collision warning with pedestrian detection and automatic emergency braking, blind-spot monitors, rear cross-traffic alert, adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, lane-departure warning, front and rear parking sensors, reverse brake assist, and a 360-degree camera system. Ford’s BlueCruise driver-assist system comes standard with a three-month trial. It offers hands-free driving on thousands of miles of mapped highways. The 2026 Explorer does well in crash tests. It scores a perfect five out of five stars overall from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and earns a Top Safety Pick, the second highest honor, from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS). Pricing and Release Date Ford has not yet announced pricing for the 2027 Explorer ST Sinister Package, nor for any 2027 Explorer for that matter. However, the 2026 Ford Explorer ST starts at $56,700, including a mandatory $1,795 destination fee. Expect a price increase for the base ST for 2027 and an additional charge for the Sinister Package. The other trim levels are likely to return. They include Active, ST-Line, off-road-oriented Tremor, and luxurious Platinum. The 2027 Ford Explorer ST Sinister Package will arrive later this year. title: Operating Expenses: Meaning, Calculation, and Examples
summary: Learn more about the ins and outs of operating expenses in this comprehensive guide.
body_text: Type above and press Enter to search. Press Esc to cancel. All blogs Company Retail Restaurant Ecommerce Golf Retail Operating Expenses: Meaning, Calculation, and Examples by Lightspeed 2026-08-11 minute read Share Post Operating expenses (OPEX) are a crucial part of running a retail business. From rent and utilities to payroll and marketing, these costs directly impact your bottom line. And when margins are tight and competition is fierce, effectively managing OPEX can mean the difference between success and getting left behind. In this guide, we’ll break down what operating expenses are, why they matter and how you can manage them efficiently in today’s evolving retail landscape. What are operating expenses? Why are operating expenses important for businesses? Capital expenses vs operating expenses: what’s the difference? Common challenges in managing operating expenses How do you calculate OPEX and CAPEX? How to track CAPEX and OPEX What are some examples of retail operating expenses? What’s excluded from operating expenses? How to Track and Manage Operating Expenses What’s going to happen with retail operating costs in 2026? Preparing for rising retail operating expenses Searching for the right POS system? Our free guide will help you understand the kind of point-of-sale system you need to run your business efficiently. View the guide Key takeaways Operating expenses (OPEX) are the ongoing costs required to run a business, such as rent, utilities, payroll, marketing, software subscriptions, and office supplies. OPEX differs from capital expenditures (CAPEX), which are long-term investments in assets like equipment, property, or technology that provide value over multiple years. OPEX also differs from cost of goods sold (COGS), which includes the direct costs of producing or acquiring products sold to customers. Common examples of operating expenses include employee salaries, insurance, professional services, advertising, and facility maintenance. Tracking operating expenses helps businesses understand profitability, manage cash flow, and identify opportunities to reduce costs. High operating expenses can reduce operating income and profit margins, while efficient expense management can improve overall financial performance. Monitoring OPEX regularly allows businesses to create more accurate budgets and make informed strategic decisions. What are operating expenses? Operating expenses include all the ongoing costs a business incurs to maintain its daily operations. Unlike capital expenses (CAPEX), which involve long-term investments like equipment or real estate, OPEX covers essential recurring costs such as rent, utilities, salaries and marketing expenses. Is inventory an operating expense? Is inventory an operating expense? It’s a bit tricky. When you sell an item, its cost moves to Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) . But before the sale, inventory is an asset on your balance sheet. Inventory isn’t just finished goods, though; it also includes raw materials, transportation, manufacturing, storage and other overhead costs. Why are operating expenses important for businesses? Managing OPEX effectively is a key part of maintaining a healthy bottom line, improving operational efficiency and staying competitive in evolving markets. Uncontrolled expenses can quickly eat into your profit margins, especially in industries like retail, where costs can fluctuate due to external factors like inflation, supply chain disruptions and shifting consumer demand. But a well-optimized OPEX strategy can allow retailers to allocate resources strategically—investing in areas that drive growth, including the customer experience , digital transformation and employee development. By keeping operating expenses in check, businesses can remain agile and boost cash flow, ensuring they have the flexibility to seize new opportunities, whether expanding into new markets or investing in more innovative technologies. Capital expenses vs operating expenses: what’s the difference? Understanding business expenses can be a challenge for many retailers, whether they’re in the planning stages of launching a new venture or actively managing the finances of an existing business. They fall into two basic categories: OPEX and CAPEX. Here’s how they differ. Understanding CAPEX Capital expenses (CAPEX) are significant investments in assets designed to provide long-term benefits to your business. Unlike daily operating expenses, CAPEX involves acquiring or upgrading major assets like new equipment, building renovations or significant tech upgrades. These investments are planned with long-term budgets in mind, as they often require more funding and are seen as investments for future growth. Understanding OPEX As we previously mentioned, operating expenses are the costs associated with the day-to-day running of a business. Examples of operating expenses include employee salaries, rent, utilities and marketing initiatives. COGS vs OPEX Think of COGS as the price tag on creating your product—it covers direct costs like raw materials and production labor. Operating expenses, on the other hand, keep the business running smoothly, covering essentials like rent and utilities. While COGS is tied to making your product, OPEX is not directly tied to production. Category CAPEX OPEX COGS Definition Long-term investments in business assets Day-to-day costs of running the business Direct costs associated with producing, purchasing, or delivering goods sold to customers Purpose Supports future growth and expansion Keeps the business operational Measures the direct cost of generating revenue from product sales Examples New equipment, building renovations, major tech upgrades Salaries, rent, utilities, marketing Raw materials, inventory purchases, manufacturing labor, shipping costs related to products sold Budgeting Requires long-term planning and higher funding Covered by regular operational budgets Fluctuates based on sales volume and production needs Accounting treatment Depreciated over time Fully expensed in the year incurred Recorded as an expense when the related goods are sold Common challenges in managing operating expenses Managing operating expenses isn’t always as simple as it seems. Businesses often encounter several complex challenges that can impact their bottom line: Budgeting and forecasting challenges: Predicting future expenses accurately is difficult, especially in a fluctuating economy. Unexpected costs, such as supplier price increases or higher energy bills, can throw off even the most well-planned budgets. Balancing cost control with quality and customer service: Cutting costs too aggressively can impact product quality and the customer experience, leading to lost sales and damage to your brand. Retailers must find a balance between cost efficiency and maintaining high standards. Dealing with fluctuating costs: Operating costs such as rent, utilities and wages are often influenced by external factors like inflation and economic shifts. Businesses need to adopt flexible budgeting strategies to adapt to these changes while trying to minimize financial strain. How do you calculate OPEX and CAPEX? Retailers can calculate OPEX and CAPEX using the following formulas. Understanding the difference between OPEX and CAPEX helps retailers make smarter financial decisions. When calculating OPEX, you’re looking at the recurring costs that keep your business running, while CAPEX calculations focus on long-term investments that add value over time. By analyzing these expenses separately, retailers can better manage cash flow and plan for growth. How to track CAPEX and OPEX If you’re not already using accounting software to track expenses, now’s a great time to start! Tools like QuickBooks can help categorize every transaction, making it easier to distinguish between operating expenses and capital expenditures. Regularly tracking and reviewing expenses ensures you know where cash is flowing and helps with budgeting and forecasting. Separating OPEX and CAPEX in your budget allows for better organization and prioritization. OPEX gives a real-time snapshot of financial health, while CAPEX planning ensures sustainable growth. Retailers should also consider industry-specific expenses. Ecommerce businesses might save on rent but spend more on IT and shipping, while brick-and-mortar stores have physical location costs but may not need as much digital infrastructure. By tracking expenses effectively, retailers can optimize operations, reduce unnecessary costs and make informed financial decisions that drive long-term success. How to track capital expenses Capital expenditures require a different approach than operating expenses. CAPEX consists of long-term expenses such as maintenance and anything that involves investments for future growth. As a result, capital expenses require long-term budgetary planning. Think of this as tracking future projects for growth. Tracking CAPEX involves creating deadlines, identifying the scope of the project and accounting for budgetary needs. Include important details such as materials, funding requirements, labor costs and other necessary information. Accounting software , rather than manual bookkeeping, will give you more freedom when mapping out your capital expenses. How to track operating expenses Spreadsheets can be a good starting point for tracking business expenses when you first open your new venture. But as you scale and your expenses become more complicated, you’ll need a more sophisticated way of tracking your expenses. That’s where accounting software comes in once again: not only will you save time on bookkeeping, but you’ll get a better overview of your expenses compared to your overall revenue. This can help you understand where you need to cut costs, and how to streamline your expenses to maximize revenue. If you’re transitioning from Excel spreadsheets to a software that comprehensively tracks expenses, don’t stress about losing data. These sheets can easily be imported to most accounting software. By eliminating manual entry of your daily and monthly expenses, you’ll reduce the risk of errors and make your life (and your accountant’s life!) much simpler when it comes to tax time. What are some examples of retail operating expenses? Not all operating expenses are created equal; some drive revenue, while others keep the business running smoothly. Direct expenses, like sales commissions, are tied directly to making money. Indirect expenses, such as office supplies, support daily operations but don’t generate revenue on their own. The good news? As long as they meet tax guidelines, both can be tax-deductible, helping to lower your taxable income. Salaries Salaries are one of the largest examples of operating expenses in retail. This includes wages for store associates, managers, cashiers, and support staff, along with payroll taxes, benefits, commissions, and training costs. Staffing expenses ensure smooth store operations and consistent customer service. Store rent Store rent covers the cost of occupying physical retail space. This may include monthly lease payments, property taxes, and common area maintenance fees depending on the lease agreement. Rent is a fixed expense that plays a major role in a retailer’s cost structure. Marketing and ad spend Marketing and advertising expenses include digital ads, social media campaigns, email marketing, in-store promotions, and seasonal campaigns. These costs help drive traffic, increase brand awareness, and generate sales across both physical and online channels. Product deliveries Product delivery expenses cover the transportation of inventory from suppliers to warehouses and stores. This includes shipping fees, freight costs, and last-mile delivery services required to keep shelves stocked and operations running smoothly. Utilities Utilities include essential services such as electricity, water, gas, internet, and phone services. These recurring costs are necessary to maintain store operations, lighting, climate control, and communication systems. Insurance premiums, legal and accounting fees Retailers also incur costs for business insurance, which protects against risks like property damage and liability claims. In addition, legal and accounting fees cover professional services such as tax preparation, bookkeeping, compliance, and contract support. Maintenance and Repairs Maintenance and repair costs ensure that store facilities, equipment, and systems remain in good working condition. This includes HVAC servicing, equipment repairs, cleaning services, and general facility upkeep. What’s excluded from operating expenses? Operating expenses do not typically include one-time costs such as capital investments or long-term debt payments. These business costs, and a range of others, are what are known as non-operating expenses. Understanding non-operating expenses Non-operating expenses are not related to a company’s core business operations. These can include: Fees for legal services Charges for interest on loans Gains or losses from asset sales Non-operating expenses still need to be monitored closely, so you can make financial decisions and accurately calculate your business’ earnings. How to Track and Manage Operating Expenses When it comes to overseeing your operating expenses, one of the most important things to do is manage your budget efficiently. Here are a few ways to effectively manage your operating expenses: Take advantage of low-cost marketing methods, such as email outreach and social media posts. Remove third-party providers and embrace technology to cut costs by using an integrated POS system and payments platform , like Lightspeed. Assess areas where you can reduce waste. Review all subscriptions and cancel anything redundant or unused. Be efficient–regularly review supplier contracts and streamline operations to reduce costs without sacrificing quality. What’s going to happen with retail operating costs in 2026? Retailers in 2026 are facing a rapidly changing landscape influenced by economic uncertainty, shifting consumer behavior and technological advancements. As costs continue to rise in key areas, businesses must stay ahead of trends to manage expenses effectively while maintaining profitability and customer satisfaction. AI and automation will reshape cost structures According to McKinsey , artificial intelligence and automation are expected to play an even greater role in retail operations, from inventory management and demand forecasting to customer service and marketing. AI-powered tools can help retailers optimize staffing levels, reduce waste, and streamline supply chain processes—all of which can contribute to lower operating costs. Sustainability will become a financial necessity Sustainable business practices are no longer just about corporate responsibility—they are becoming essential cost-saving strategies. Retailers are investing in energy-efficient solutions, waste reduction programs and sustainable sourcing to meet consumer demand while cutting long-term operational costs. The rise of hybrid shopping experiences The integration of ecommerce and brick-and-mortar retail is continuing to evolve, requiring retailers to invest in omnichannel strategies . However, maintaining multiple sales channels comes with additional operational expenses, including digital platform fees, logistics and fulfillment costs. Labor shortages and rising wages Labor costs are expected to increase due to ongoing workforce shortages and new regulations around fair wages. Deloitte predicts that retailers will need to find innovative ways to attract and retain employees while managing payroll expenses. Supply chain volatility will drive up costs Retailers continue to navigate unpredictable supply chain challenges , including shipping delays, raw material price fluctuations and geopolitical disruptions. This volatility requires businesses to reassess sourcing strategies, build stronger supplier relationships, and invest in inventory optimization technologies. Preparing for rising retail operating expenses A well-defined budget ensures all operating expenses are covered while keeping the business profitable. It’s essential to account for seasonal fluctuations, market changes, and unexpected costs to maintain financial stability. As costs rise, retailers often face tough decisions— increase prices or accept lower profit margins . To make informed choices, business owners should analyze industry performance metrics and key indicators . Understanding market trends helps retailers stay competitive while balancing pricing strategies and profitability. Proactively tracking these factors ensures smarter financial planning and long-term success. If you’d like to explore how Lightspeed can help you manage your operating expenses and grow your retail business, talk to one of our experts . FAQs on operating expenses Is income tax expense an operating expense? No, income tax expense is not considered an operating expense. It’s classified as a non-operating expense because it’s not directly related to a company’s core business operations. Operating expenses typically include day-to-day costs like rent, salaries and utilities—not taxes owed on profits. Is operating expense a liability or asset? Operating expenses are neither liabilities nor assets. Instead, they are recorded as expenses on the income statement. They represent the costs a business incurs to keep operations running smoothly and are fully expensed in the period in which they occur. How do operating costs affect profit? Operating costs directly impact your bottom line. The higher your operating expenses, the lower your operating profit will be—unless your revenue increases proportionally. Keeping OPEX under control helps businesses maintain healthy margins and free up cash flow for growth initiatives. Are operating expenses included in COGS? No, operating expenses and Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) are separate. COGS includes the direct costs of producing goods (like raw materials and labor tied to manufacturing), while operating expenses cover the broader costs of running the business—such as rent, utilities and marketing. Are wages operating expenses? Yes, wages are considered operating expenses. Salaries and employee benefits are typically among the largest operating costs for a retail business. These expenses fall under the category of day-to-day costs necessary to keep the business functioning. What does an increase in operating expenses mean? An increase in operating expenses can signal higher costs of doing business—due to inflation, rising wages, supply chain issues, or expansion. While some increases may support growth (like marketing investments), unchecked OPEX can reduce profitability if not managed strategically. How do operating costs affect selling price? Operating costs directly influence a product’s selling price because businesses must price their goods high enough to cover expenses like rent, salaries, marketing, and utilities while still maintaining profit margins. When operating costs increase, retailers often raise prices to preserve profitability. Conversely, lower operating costs can allow for more competitive pricing or improved margins. Ultimately, selling price reflects both production costs and ongoing operating expenses, making cost management essential for pricing strategy. title: 7 Proven Strategies to Bring New Customers into Your Dispensary in 2026
summary: 7 proven tactics to bring new customers into your dispensary in 2026, from AI search visibility and SEO to referrals and community partnerships.
body_text: Attracting new customers starts before any marketing campaign: a strong product selection, great service, and a consistent brand. That foundation is what turns a first visit into a repeat customer and a word-of-mouth referral. It matters even more in 2026, since cannabis retailers still can't rely on mainstream paid ads. Most shoppers find their next dispensary through Google, AI assistants, personal recommendations, and the channels you already own: your customer data, your website and menu, your loyalty program, and your presence in the community. Here are seven tactics that reach specific types of shoppers, all built on channels you control. In This Post 1. Enhance Your Online Presence, SEO, and AI Search Visibility 2. Utilize Targeted Cannabis Dispensary Marketing Campaigns 3. Offer First-Time Customer Discounts and Promotions 4. Build Local Goodwill: Events, Workshops, and Community Partnerships 5. Implement a Dispensary Loyalty Program 6. Launch a Customer Referral Program 7. Leverage Social Media Platforms Common Questions 1. Enhance Your Online Presence, SEO, and AI Search Visibility Attracting: Search-First Shoppers and Tech-Savvy Millennials Most new customers find a dispensary in 2026 by searching Google or asking an AI assistant. Show up there, and you win the visit. Keep your site fast, mobile-friendly, and full of content that answers real customer questions rather than pure promotional copy. SEO fundamentals: Claim and complete your Google Business Profile: hours, categories, service area, photos. Host a live, keyword-rich menu on your own domain, not just a third-party marketplace. Build a steady stream of genuine reviews across Google, Weedmaps, and Leafly. AI search visibility: AI tools don't crawl your site in real time. They draw on what's already indexed, so consistency and structure matter more than ever: Keep your name, address, phone number, and hours identical across your website, Google Business Profile, Weedmaps, Leafly, and Yelp. Add LocalBusiness and FAQ schema to your site so AI systems can extract your content accurately. Lead each page and FAQ with a direct one-to-two-sentence answer before adding detail. For more, read Dispensary SEO: The Truth About E-Commerce, Google Rankings, and Online Sales. How Meadow supports this: Menu Pro puts a customizable, live menu on your own domain instead of a third-party marketplace, so every visit builds your site's authority. Along with SEO+, Meadow's built-in suite of technical SEO tools that automatically optimizes page speed, product metadata, and sitemaps, so your menu is structured to rank without needing a web team to manage it. Weedmaps is cannabis retail's largest marketplace, so a strong presence there matters. The Weedmaps integration keeps that listing accurate automatically, with live menu updates and orders routing straight back into your POS. But treat it as the front door, not the destination : Weedmaps also makes it easy for a shopper to tap straight over to a competitor, so once you've won a first-time customer there, give them a reason to order directly from your own site next time. Edge (formerly EyeRate) rewards your team for earning genuine positive reviews, the same signal that helps both search rankings and AI citations. 2. Utilize Targeted Cannabis Dispensary Marketing Campaigns Attracting: Canna-sseurs and Brand Loyal Customers Targeted campaigns are the highest-return channel a dispensary controls, because they reach people who've already opted in. Personalized messages based on purchase history and preferences consistently outperform one-size-fits-all blasts. Run campaigns across the channels cannabis is actually allowed to use: Email: Personalized newsletters aligned with purchase history, via our API partner Alpine IQ . SMS: Instant flash-sale and exclusive-deal alerts, segmented by purchase history, loyalty status, or VIP tier. Text marketing is one of the highest-converting channels available, since it only reaches customers who explicitly opted in. Weedmaps Deals: Advertise deals on your Weedmaps listing to reach new brand-loyal customers, then track which products those shoppers buy to refine future offers. How Meadow supports this: Meadow's built-in text messaging tool sends SMS campaigns directly from that same data, no separate platform required, and its Digital Flyer feature works around carrier filtering on cannabis-specific language. Prefer a dedicated CRM layered on top? Alpine IQ is also available as an API partner. 3. Offer First-Time Customer Discounts and Promotions Attracting: Bargain Hunters and New Cannabis Users A first-time discount is often the deciding factor for a shopper comparing dispensaries, and it opens the door to loyalty enrollment down the line. The key is making offers compelling enough to get people through the door but sustainable for your margins. See How to Build a Dispensary Discount Strategy for the margin math. Percentage or Dollars Off: A simple, transparent first-visit discount. BOGO or Bundled Deals: Introduce new customers to more of your catalog while growing basket size. Gift with Purchase: A small sample or branded merch above a minimum spend. 4. Build Local Goodwill: Events, Workshops, and Community Partnerships Attracting: Community-Oriented Customers, Newbies, and Enthusiasts Showing up locally builds a kind of trust no ad can buy, and it compounds year over year. That can mean educational workshops for beginners, deeper-dive sessions on cultivation or terpenes for enthusiasts, sponsoring local events, or simply partnering with nearby businesses. Each one gives your dispensary real value to offer beyond a transaction, and each one strengthens your reputation as a knowledgeable, community-invested business. Case study: Posh Green Cannabis Boutique , San Francisco's first equity retail cannabis dispensary independently owned by a woman of color, Reese Benton, has built community service into its business model since its founding in 2016. On January 19, 2023, Posh Green partnered with PAX and other local businesses to host a Day of Peace compassion event , distributing free cannabis products to veterans, LGBTQ+ individuals, and trauma survivors under the Dennis Peron and Brownie Mary Act (SB-34), which permits tax-free cannabis donations to low-income California patients. That kind of visible, values-aligned commitment is what turns community members into loyal customers. How Meadow supports this: Dynamic Delivery lets you extend your presence beyond your storefront, setting up temporary kiosks and a delivery zone at a partner venue or event so you can serve and educate attendees on the spot without carrying physical inventory into the space. 5. Implement a Dispensary Loyalty Program Attracting: Repeat Customers and Value Seekers Loyalty programs turn a first visit into a habit, rewarding repeat customers with points, discounts, or exclusive deals. They're also a new-customer tool: shoppers comparing two dispensaries often choose the one where their spending earns something back. How Meadow supports this: Meadow's loyalty program offers flexible rewards (cash back, flat or percent discounts, free products), points that redeem anywhere customers shop, and built-in single-use promo codes for targeted campaigns. 6. Launch a Customer Referral Program Attracting: Friends and Family of Existing Customers Referrals solve a problem loyalty programs don't: they reward a customer for bringing someone new in, not just for shopping again themselves. In a market where paid acquisition is mostly off-limits, turning existing customers into your sales force is one of the highest-leverage moves available, and it costs you only what you'd already be discounting anyway. Keep it simple: give both the referring customer and their new friend a reward, redeemable on the new customer's first purchase. A flat discount or a free gift both work; what matters is that the offer is easy to explain in one sentence and easy to redeem in-store. How Meadow supports this: Meadow's built-in, single-use promo codes make referral tracking straightforward: issue a unique code to a customer, share it however you like (text, email, in-store), and redeem it directly at checkout with no separate referral platform needed. 7. Leverage Social Media Platforms Attracting: Young Adults and Social Media Enthusiasts Social media builds the brand that makes every other channel work harder, even though cannabis businesses still can't run paid ads on the major platforms. As of 2026, platforms still restrict cannabis content, and accounts get flagged for violating community guidelines. A few precautions to avoid getting shadow-banned: Be mindful of your hashtags Avoid showing the plant or consumption Highlight scientific research instead Diversify your content and don't post excessively Follow each platform's community guidelines Don't advertise anything that could draw children's attention By combining these tactics with quality products, great service, and a strong brand, dispensary owners can attract new customers and build a loyal base for long-term growth. Common Questions How do dispensaries attract new customers? Dispensaries attract new customers most reliably through channels they own and control: a search- and AI-optimized website, targeted email and text campaigns, first-time discounts, loyalty and referral programs, community events, and compliant social media. Paid advertising remains heavily restricted for cannabis, so owned channels outperform. How do I get my dispensary recommended by AI tools like ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews? Keep your name, address, phone number, and hours identical across your website, Google Business Profile, Weedmaps, Leafly, and Yelp, add LocalBusiness and FAQ schema to your site, and build a steady stream of genuine reviews. AI tools draw on indexed, consistent information rather than crawling your site in real time. Do referral programs work for dispensaries? Yes, especially where paid advertising is restricted. A referral program turns existing customers into an acquisition channel, rewarding them for bringing in someone new rather than just for shopping again. Keep the offer simple and easy to redeem in one visit. Can dispensaries advertise on Google or Instagram? As of the writing of this article, mainstream platforms like Google, Meta, and Instagram still broadly prohibit paid cannabis advertising, and organic accounts risk removal for showing products or consumption. Focus on organic SEO, AI search visibility, your own website and menu, review generation, and opt-in email and SMS instead. Ready to Fill Your Door with New Customers? Every strategy in this post runs better on a POS built for cannabis marketing: customer profiles from the first visit, targeted campaigns, loyalty and referrals, and analytics that show which channel actually drove the sale. Meadow has been building cannabis retail software since 2014 and is the #1-rated cannabis POS on G2, 4.9/5 as of July 2026.
