title: Event Guest List Management for B2B Teams: A Complete Guide | Zuddl Blog
summary: A practical guide to B2B guest list management: nominations, approvals, and follow-up. Includes an honest look at Airtable and other guest list management tools
body_text: [.ebook-q-card][.ebook-body-text] TL;DR : For B2B teams managing guest lists for their events, the data needed to nominate, approve, and follow up on the right people lives in different systems and becomes stale between each handoff. A spreadsheet can't display all the context that needs to be visible at the point of decision. We cover what the current tool landscape is, what an ideal b2b guest list needs to have, and what you should look out for when evaluating platforms. [.ebook-body-text][.ebook-q-card] Row 47 of 214. A VP has the event guest list open in one tab and Salesforce open in another. The name in that row has no account tier next to it, and no deal stage. There is a nomination note an AE left three weeks ago: “good fit, per rep”. That tells them nothing. The VP alt-tabs to Salesforce, searches the company, scans the account history, alt-tabs back, and types "approved." The spreadsheet had a name, a company, an email. What it also needed was context to make the nomination decision instant. This is crucial because when you’re holding limited capacity events, you want the right people in the room. What does event guest list management look like for a B2B team? The context problem only compounds at scale. For a program running a field event in one region, a partner roadshow in another, and an executive dinner series on top of both, row 47 is just one row on one of a dozen lists open at once, each with its own approval chain and its own AEs nominating into it. Most teams manage guest lists for their event on a spreadsheet plus Salesforce plus Slack plus Marketo. A few have used Zapier automations for CRM syncs, or a tool like Clay to enrich contacts before nominations. Some built a custom report for approval context. While these workarounds help with data freshness, they don’t fully solve the issue of collaboration and visibility. The event marketer becomes the person everyone routes through: AEs ask them whether their nomination got approved, the regional lead asking why a different region's list is moving faster, the rep asking if a lead from last month's event is still worth calling. This coordination tax is the single biggest operational drain in event marketing. In Momentus's Q1 2026 survey of event leaders, 42% named manual coordination across teams as the one burden they'd eliminate first. You could potentially have several lists moving at once, and you’re still chasing leads from last month’s event even as the list for the next event starts to be built. Unlike a content calendar or a budget tracker where a slight delay doesn’t change the usefulness of the sheet, a B2B event guest list demands constant synchronisation. For a particular account, the deal might move a stage, which would impact why a particular lead should or shouldn’t be invited to an event. The follow-up only matters within the window before a lead goes cold, and it’s a short window of 48-72 hours. Solving this isn’t easy because the data that’s needed exists in multiple places.The CRM has account and deal data. Communication and coordination happens over multiple Slack or email threads, and the spreadsheet has the guest list itself. The event marketer ends up patching the seam between all three. What are the three stages of B2B guest list management? There are three main stages an event guest list moves through. When managed via a spreadsheet, there can be versioning, live sync, or visibility issues: ‍ List building or nominations: An event marketer pulls a base list from the CRM, then account executives, and sales leadership send their additions. This could be in the form of a Slack message, a separate spreadsheet with different column headers, an email with a name and nothing else. There is no guarantee that it gets saved properly, or even in the same format. This can also become a question of data quality. Is the same person already sitting somewhere else in the CRM as a lead, a contact, or an account record under a different name? Someone has to merge, deduplicate, and reconcile whatever comes back into one format. By the time that’s done, the list is days old and some leads might even have switched jobs. ‍ Approvals: A person with sign-off authority, often a VP or a sales leader, has to look at a list of names and decide who gets invited. Without account tier, deal stage, or a note on who nominated the person and why, that decision often gets made on whatever weak signal is available instead. This can take upto 45 minutes per batch because they have to look up the lead in the CRM separately, and often the approver comes back to the event marketer with questions. This is also complicated by CRM hygiene and accuracy. 76% of organizations say less than half their CRM data is accurate and complete, which means an approver has to spend extra time looking for the right context, and if they don’t find it, come back to the events team with questions. Guest list management can mean a lot of stringing data sources together for context Sometimes, the loss of signal is deliberate. At some orgs, executive contacts are maintained outside the CRM because these contacts need peer relationships - they won’t talk to an AE, so it’s another list in a separate system. Either way, the approval is slower and less reliable than it needs to be. ‍ Lead follow-up: After leads get assigned to reps, the spreadsheet has no way to show whether a rep called, emailed, or did nothing. CEIR estimates that 80% of trade show leads never get followed up at all. The events team has to manually chase the reps. A senior event marketing manager at an enterprise SaaS company described this as: "basically us hounding them all after the meeting... we have a Slack channel that we'll do for events and we'll just tell them to put their notes in the Slack channel. We go find them." What types of tools can B2B teams use for guest list management? Approach CRM data freshness Context at approval Follow-up visibility External collaborator access Plain spreadsheet, manual export Stale as soon as the underlying CRM record changes None. The approver looks it up elsewhere None. Surfaces at the debrief Full sheet access, or none Airtable with native Salesforce sync Refreshes roughly hourly, one direction only Not built in Not built in No native field-hiding Dedicated guest-list or registration vendor with real-time sync Updates as registrations happen, for registration data only No, as per public materials No, as per public materials Role-based. Full role or no access. No column-level control Live-synced table, built for B2B event guest lists (Zuddl Smart Tables) Live. The row stays connected to the record Visible in the row Yes Column-level. External collaborators verify by email and see only the columns opened to them, no license required ‍ Most B2B event teams managing guest lists might already be familiar with these types of tools. Each of them have a limit, and the limit you accept depends on the maturity of your event program: Plain spreadsheets : eg. Google Sheets, Excel are where nearly every team starts, because they’re the simplest. No procurement, no training, total flexibility over columns and formatting. These are great but require a lot of manual effort to maintain. Flexible no-code databases: like Airtable and Notion have tables that link to each other, so a guest record ties to a company record instead of getting retyped on every row, saveable filtered views, and often some form of CRM sync. Here are some of the limitations you might run into when building your guest list via these tools: Airtable's native Salesforce sync is gated to higher-tier plans and is only one way: changes made to the base table aren’t automatically reflected in the CRM. a name approved or annotated inside the base still has to be updated in the CRM by hand. Notion has no native CRM sync at all. Sync mechanics vary by CRM and by tool Volume limits are common on integrated syncs. Airtable has a 10,000 record cap Nothing events-specific gets built on top of the database. Someone has to manually build the approval logic, keep the records updated both in the table and the CRM and email or Slack the sales teams to follow up Dedicated guest-list and event-registration vendors Each solve one piece well: Splash is a design-led event marketing platform built for branded event pages and registration at scale, with CRM sync that pushes registration data to Salesforce or HubSpot. It doesn't answer whether a specific person on the guest list should be approved based on their context Invitario is good at on-site VIP handling, identifying and flagging VIP guests as they arrive, backed by role-based access control. Its public materials don't describe any CRM sync, live or otherwise. Sweap does team collaboration on a shared list, through role-based permissions, although those permissions don’t allow filtered visibility - it’s all or nothing. InviteDesk covers registration status updating in the CRM as it happens Nobody describes an approval step gated on deal-stage or account-tier context or a mechanism for tracking post-event follow-up. None of them was built to carry a name through nomination, approval, and follow-up as one connected record or provide a mechanism to handle visibility across an event program. Purpose-built, live-synced tools are the newest category. These are ‘smart tables’ where guest data stays connected to its source system instead of getting exported into a static copy. Two-thirds of event teams have already integrated their event marketing platform with their wider sales and marketing stack. This category of tools are extremely useful for such teams. How do you evaluate a guest list management tool for B2B events? Now that we’ve seen the different categories of tools for B2B guest list management, here are four questions that can help you check a vendor’s claims: Does the sync update fast enough for same-day approval, or does it lag behind the point where the decision has to get made? Can the person approving a name see current account data without opening a second tab? Can an outside collaborator, an agency or a sponsor who isn't in the CRM's own user list, get access to just the columns they need without a full license? Is there any visibility into follow up or does that question wait for the debrief the way it always has? Another question to ask yourself is: will this new tool make my process any easier, and how many tools does it replace? For teams evaluating the registration and ticketing layer specifically, alongside guest list management, a broader comparison of B2B registration platforms might be useful. How can you audit your B2B guest list management process? If you’re running an events program with more than a handful of events a year, this is less about spreadsheet hygiene and more about having one version of truth. Try these 4 steps to check which areas of your process need improvement: How long does it take to get a clean list for nominations? On the next event, or the next two or three running in parallel across regions, time how long it takes to reconcile nominations from AEs, partners, and sales leadership into one clean, deduplicated format. If it’s more than a day per list, or if there’s any manual cross-checking to make sure the same contact isn't in two separate regional lists, your guest list data is probably stale by the time you’re ready for approvals. Ask the last five approvers what they had to look up Go back to the last five people who approved a guest list and ask what they needed to check before signing off, and where they had to go find it. If the answer is "Salesforce, in another tab" more than once, or if approvals commonly take more than a day to clear, you have a context problem. Check whether anyone can answer "did the rep follow up" before the debrief meeting If the answer requires pulling a Salesforce report or asking each rep individually, you need better follow-up visibility. Count how many separate spreadsheets exist right now for partial access Every agency, sponsor, or outside collaborator who needs a full seat or a separate spreadsheet to see even part of the list is a sign that access is costing you more than it should. What columns should a B2B event guest list have? Before evaluating a tool to manage your B2B event guest , it's worth looking at what an ideal B2B event guest management list should contain. Column Source Who needs to see it Notes Contact name CRM or nomination Everyone Company CRM or nomination Everyone Email CRM or nomination Internal, plus agency if sending invites Job title/seniority CRM or nomination Everyone People change jobs – check this first Company size/industry CRM Everyone Together with job title, used to assess fit Nominator Manual (AE, partner, sales leader) Internal only Who submitted this name and why Nomination reason Manual Internal only Why this person for this event Account tier CRM Approver Needs to be live Deal stage CRM Approver Stale deal stage is worse than no deal stage Invite tier/priority Manual/workflow Internal Segment into tier lists based on who you want in the room Approval status Workflow or manual Internal Approved, rejected, or pending RSVP status Registration system Internal, plus agency Confirmed, declined, or no response Event history CRM (campaign membership) Internal Was this person at the dinner in March? The roadshow in June? Follow-up status CRM or manual Sales and event marketer Contacted, not yet, or no response after X days Follow-up owner CRM Sales and event marketer Which rep owns the post-event action ‍ When each column needs to be surfaced Not every column needs to be visible at each stage. This is where each column is most useful, mapped to the stages mentioned earlier. The line isn’t this clear or defined (eg. much of the information that’s valuable at the approval stage can also inform a nomination), but in general: At nomination : contact name, company, email, job title, nominator, nomination reason. This is everything an AE can supply without leaving the row. If they have to go find any of it, nominations slow down. At approval : account tier, deal stage, company size, event history, invite tier. The CRM columns should populate on their own, and this is the only moment they become useful. After the invite goes out : RSVP status. After the event : follow-up owner, then follow-up status. The ability to track event history turns a per-event list into a program-level asset, because it answers "have we already engaged this account this quarter" before anyone nominates them into a second or third program without realizing it. Right now this might exist at a per-campaign level in your systems. If any external collaborator, an agency or a sponsor will see part of this list, decide which columns they can access before sharing it. Deal stage and account tier in particular shouldn't leave the company without a deliberate reason. What a smart solution for B2B guest list management looks like Imagine if your events platform treated nomination, approval, and follow-up as steps built on top of one connected record. Instead of three separate handoffs, you’d have one live table that acts as the source of truth for your event guest list. That’s what you get with Zuddl’s Smart Tables. What Smart Tables changes CRM data is always synced in every row when you open the table: Account tier, deal stage, rep notes, and engagement history populate from Salesforce and update as the source updates. No export, no re-import, no "is this still accurate" before a decision. AEs nominate with context already in front of them: When an AE adds a name, they can see deal stage and account history before they submit Approvers see CRM context in the same view as the name: Your VP doesn’t have to alt-tab to Salesforce. You can build custom approval flows based on how your team decides Define your ideal guest and score each row against that criteria: Describe what a strong fit looks like and Smart Tables scores every row against it. A web research column fills in what the CRM might not have, such as recent job changes or funding rounds No extra licence needed for collaborators: An agency or sponsor verifies by email and sees only the columns explicitly opened to them, without a licence. Follow-up tracking for leads: Leads get assigned to reps in the same table where nominations started. An agent monitors Salesforce for each rep's activity, nudges them before the follow-up SLA closes, and escalates to the sales manager if it passes. Every status (contacted, meeting booked, no response) is visible in the table before anyone has to ask. What this means for your events program When the data is live and self-serve in one table, the questions that currently route through the event marketer (did my nomination get approved, who nominated this person, did the rep follow up) answer themselves. They can focus on which event formats are converting, and whether the program mix needs to shift. The quality of the room improves because everything from nominations to the final guest list is based on prior context. You’re able to narrow in on the 30 leads that are strong fits for your criteria from the pool of nominees. So, for example, you’d know that every invite is going to a Director-level persona at a company that employs 1000+ people and is dealing with a problem you can solve. Unlike a spreadsheet, every decision taken in the smart table triggers an action - an approval leads to an invite, and if an invite tier doesn’t fill up, the system moves on to the next tier. You define an SLA and the sales reps are nudged to follow-up before the lead goes cold. There’s no confusion about which reps own which contacts, and what they’ve done since the event ended. The platform takes on the job of being the connective tissue, and the events team gains a level of visibility it never consistently had because they’re not just executing anymore. The friction between sales and marketing drops, and debriefs are no longer about fact finding. Your baseline shifts from “did this happen” to what decisions need to be taken based on which regions and formats are working and which aren’t. Your events program starts to build on itself. If you want to see this in action for your own guest list, talk to us. {{demo-widget-1}} Frequently asked questions What's the difference between guest list management for B2B events and for weddings or consumer events? Consumer and wedding guest list tools are built around RSVP counts, meal choices, and seating arrangements. B2B guest list management centers on a different set of problems: nominations that need to be merged from multiple sources, approvals that require CRM context to make a fast decision, and follow-up that has to be visible to a sales team, not just an event host. Can I use Airtable for B2B event guest list management? Yes, and many teams do, particularly as a step up from a plain spreadsheet. Airtable's native Salesforce sync, available on Business and Enterprise Scale plans, pulls CRM records in automatically on roughly an hourly refresh, but it only runs one way: nothing entered in Airtable writes back to Salesforce. Airtable also doesn't include a built-in, events-specific approval workflow or post-event follow-up tracking, so a team still has to build or bolt on that layer itself. How do I connect Salesforce data to an event guest list spreadsheet? Most teams handle this by exporting a Salesforce report into Google Sheets, importing a Salesforce report directly, or setting up a scheduled export, all variations on the same underlying task: getting CRM fields into the spreadsheet without manually retyping them. Each approach still produces a snapshot that goes stale the moment the underlying Salesforce record changes, the core limitation they share. Is it safe to share CRM fields like deal stage or account tier in a guest list spreadsheet with external approvers or agencies? It depends entirely on how access is controlled. A spreadsheet shared broadly exposes every column to everyone with the link, including CRM fields that shouldn't leave the company. Tools with column-level permissions let a team share only the columns an outside collaborator needs, such as name and company, while keeping deal stage, account tier, and other CRM fields restricted to internal approvers. How do you handle a guest list change or cancellation after approval has already happened? This is where the staleness problem shows up again after the fact: a name approved on Monday can be irrelevant by Thursday if the account churns, the contact changes roles, or the deal falls through. Static spreadsheets have no way to flag that the underlying data moved after the approval was recorded. A guest list connected to a live data source can surface the change instead of leaving an approved name sitting on a list that's already wrong. Does this apply if we use HubSpot instead of Salesforce? Yes. The three-stage workflow (nomination, approval, follow-up) is CRM-agnostic. Sync mechanics differ by tool: Airtable's native integration is built for Salesforce, one-way and hourly, while HubSpot connections tend to run through HubSpot's own Data Sync or Workflows products on different terms. The four evaluation questions apply regardless of CRM. Check whether the tool being evaluated has a native integration for the CRM in use, and whether it runs one way or two. ‍ ‍

title: Best AI Scribe for Nurses: Shift Documentation Guide 2026
summary: Most AI scribes are built for physician visits—not nursing shifts. See what a shift-shaped scribe needs to handle timestamps, flowsheets, and handoffs.
body_text: Almost every AI scribe on the market was designed around the same thing: a 15-minute physician visit. One patient, one conversation, one note at the end. A nurse does not work like that. A shift is twelve hours, several patients at once, and documentation that accumulates the whole way through. It is not one note. It is narrative entries, flowsheets, focus charts on specific problems, and a handoff at the end that someone else has to act on. So when a tool built for an encounter gets pointed at a shift, the mismatch is structural, not cosmetic. That is the thing to evaluate, and it matters more than how many minutes a vendor claims to save. Key Takeaway: An AI scribe for nurses has to fit a shift, not an encounter. Most ambient scribes are built around a 15-minute physician visit with one patient, one problem, and one note at the end. Nursing documentation runs continuously across a 12-hour shift, spans several patients at once, moves between narrative notes, flowsheets, and focus charting, and ends in a handoff. Nurses spend roughly 25 to 40 percent of a shift documenting. The right tool also has to produce a legally defensible record, because nursing notes are the entries most often read back later: date, time, and patient identifier on every entry, late entries labelled and signed, and corrections made with a single line-through that leaves the original readable. Sully.ai's AI Scribe captures documentation during and after care and writes it into the EHR across Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth. The Shift Is the Unit of Nursing Documentation Estimates put documentation at roughly 25 to 40 percent of a nursing shift [1][2]. Nurses themselves name time pulled away from the bedside as the most demoralizing part of the job [2]. Those numbers get quoted a lot. The more useful observation is what they are measuring: not time spent on a note, but time spent on a running record that never really closes until the shift does. One Encounter Versus Twelve Hours and Six Patients A physician encounter has clean edges. It starts, it ends, and a note comes out of it. A shift has none of those edges. Six patients each generate their own timeline of assessments, interventions, responses, and escalations, interleaved across twelve hours. The documentation is not produced at the end. It accumulates, and the parts that matter most are often written in the middle of doing something else. Notes, Flowsheets, and the Handoff Nursing documentation is also not one artifact. A single shift produces narrative entries, flowsheet and vitals data, focus charts on specific problems, and a structured handoff. A tool that produces a polished narrative note and nothing else has touched one corner of the job. Why an Encounter-Shaped Scribe Fails a Shift-Shaped Job Three failure modes follow from that mismatch, and all three are testable before you buy. It Loses the Timestamp A nursing record turns on when . When the change in condition was noticed. When the provider was notified. When the intervention happened. When the patient was reassessed. A summarizer trained to produce readable prose will smooth a timeline into a paragraph. That reads nicely and destroys the most useful property of the record, which is the sequence. It Cannot Carry the Escalation Trail Provider notified, at what time, by what method, and what came back. That sequence is the first thing anyone looks for when a case is reviewed, and it is rarely a structured field in a general-purpose scribe. If the tool leaves you to type it manually every time, it has not removed the work that carries the most weight. It Has No Concept of a Correction Physician notes get amended. Nursing entries get corrected under specific rules, and a tool with no notion of a late entry or a line-through correction cannot produce a compliant record on its own. You end up working around it. What Makes a Nursing Note Legally Defensible This is the part that separates nursing documentation from most other clinical writing. Nursing entries are the minute-by-minute account of what was observed and what was done about it, which makes them the record most likely to be read back later. The rules are specific and worth knowing exactly. Date, Time, and Identifier on Every Entry Every entry is anchored with the date, the time, and the patient identifier. This is what prevents entries being attributed to the wrong patient or the wrong point in a timeline. Late Entries Are Legitimate, If Labelled Going back to document later is allowed. A late entry carries the current date and time, is labelled as a late entry, and is signed, and it should only be written if you genuinely recall the omitted information [3]. What is not allowed is quietly writing it as though it were contemporaneous. Corrections Never Erase To correct an error, draw a single line through it so the original stays readable, then date and initial the correction [3]. Deleting, overwriting, or obscuring the original destroys the integrity of the record, and a record that looks altered is worse than one that shows an honest correction. Chart Observations, Not Conclusions Write what you saw and what you did. "Patient found on floor beside bed at 0214, alert, oriented to person and place" is defensible. "Patient fell" is an inference about an event nobody witnessed. Free Nursing Note Templates These are the three formats a floor actually uses. Each has the legal guidance printed on the page, which is the part a blank text box in the EHR will never give you. Nursing narrative shift note template for end-of-shift and event documentation, with fields for provider notification, patient education, and safety Nursing SOAPIE note template for when the note needs to carry through intervention and evaluation, not stop at assessment and plan Nursing DAR focus charting note template for one problem per note, on units where charting time is tight How to Evaluate an AI Scribe for Nursing Four questions, in the order that matters. Does It Understand a Shift or Only a Visit Ask how it handles several patients across twelve hours rather than one encounter. If the demo is a single simulated visit, you have not seen it do the job. Does It Preserve Timestamps and the Escalation Sequence Give it a scenario with a change in condition, a provider notification, and a reassessment. Check whether the times survive into the output as times, or get smoothed into prose. Does It Write Into the EHR or Hand You Text A note you copy and paste is a note you handled twice, and at six patients a shift that adds up quickly. Does It Support Late Entries and Corrections Properly Ask directly. A tool that cannot label a late entry or preserve a struck-through original is not built for nursing documentation. Where Sully.ai Fits for Nursing Teams Sully's AI Scribe captures documentation during and after care and writes it into the EHR, on a single integration across Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth . Clinicians can save how they want a note structured, so the format stays consistent across a unit rather than varying by who is charting. The work around the note also comes off the floor. The AI Triage Nurse handles pre-visit intake and follow-up tracking, and the AI Receptionist handles scheduling and outreach, so the calls and coordination that land on the nursing station do not all land on a nurse. Sully operates across 5,000+ providers , has delivered 50M+ hours of AI work, and prices each AI role 80 to 90 percent below the human equivalent. There is more on how the AI nurse role works if you want the detail. Book a demo and bring a real shift, not a single visit. FAQ Q: What should an AI scribe for nurses do that a physician scribe does not? It has to fit a shift rather than an encounter. Nursing documentation runs across twelve hours and several patients, moves between narrative notes, flowsheets, and focus charting, and ends in a handoff. It also has to preserve timestamps and the escalation sequence, since a nursing record turns on when something was noticed, when the provider was notified, and when the patient was reassessed. Q: How much time do nurses spend on documentation? Estimates put it at roughly 25 to 40 percent of a shift, and nurses commonly cite documentation pulling them away from the bedside as the most demoralizing part of the job [1][2]. Q: Can an AI scribe write a legally defensible nursing note? It can help, but the rules still apply to you as the author. Every entry needs the date, time, and patient identifier. A late entry must carry the current date and time, be labelled as a late entry, and be signed. Corrections are made with a single line through the error so the original stays readable, dated and initialled, never erased [3]. Q: Which nursing note format should I use? Narrative works for end-of-shift and event documentation, SOAPIE when the note needs to carry through intervention and evaluation, and DAR focus charting when you are tracking a single problem and charting time is tight. Most units use a combination depending on the entry. Q: Do you have free nursing note templates? Yes. Sully publishes three: a narrative shift note, a SOAPIE note, and a DAR focus charting note. Each has the legal guidance printed on the page, including the late entry rule and the single line-through correction rule. Sources [1] Tandem Health — Where Nursing Documentation Time Goes [2] AICERTs — AI Scribe Technology Cuts Nursing Documentation Time [3] Nurse.com — Late Entries in Nursing Documentation: What's Allowed [4] DeepCura — Best AI Scribe for Nurses [5] Sully.ai — The AI Workforce for Healthcare

title: What Is a Transaction ID? How to Check UPI Transaction ID Status Online
summary: Need to verify a payment? Learn how to perform a Transaction ID check, find your UPI Transaction ID, understand UTR, and track payment status.
body_text: Table of Contents Toggle A Transaction ID is a unique reference number assigned to every digital payment. It helps users track payment status, verify successful transactions, resolve failed UPI payments, and assists banks or merchants in locating a specific transaction quickly. Whether you’re paying a friend via UPI, shopping online, or transferring money through net banking, every digital payment is assigned a unique Transaction ID. Think of it as a digital receipt that helps identify and track a specific payment from start to finish. If you’ve ever wondered “What is a Transaction ID?”, needed to perform a UPI transaction ID check, or contacted customer support for a failed payment, this unique identifier is usually the first thing they’ll ask for. For individuals, a Transaction ID helps verify payment status and resolve issues like pending or failed transactions. For businesses, it plays a crucial role in payment reconciliation, refunds, dispute resolution, and fraud detection. In this guide, you’ll learn what a Transaction ID is, how it works, where to find your UPI Transaction ID, and how to use it to check payment status across popular payment apps and bank platforms. What is a Transaction ID? A Transaction ID (also called Txn ID , Transaction Reference Number , or Payment Reference Number ) is a unique alphanumeric identifier generated whenever a financial transaction is initiated or completed. It acts as a reference number that allows banks, payment gateways, merchants, and customers to identify a specific payment. Every transaction receives its own unique ID, regardless of the payment method. This includes: UPI payments Credit and debit card transactions Net banking NEFT, RTGS, and IMPS transfers Digital wallets Payment gateway transactions Unlike your bank account number or UPI ID, a Transaction ID is created only for a single payment. No two completed transactions share the same identifier, making it easier to trace individual payments throughout the payment lifecycle. What information is linked to a Transaction ID? A Transaction ID is connected to key payment details such as: Transaction amount Date and time Payment status (Successful, Pending, Failed, Refunded, or Reversed) Sender and recipient details Payment method used Merchant or beneficiary information While users typically see only the reference number, banks and payment service providers use it to retrieve the complete transaction record whenever support or verification is required. Quick Answer: A Transaction ID is a one-of-a-kind reference number assigned to every digital payment. It helps users, banks, and businesses track, verify, and resolve payment-related issues. Why Do Transaction IDs Matter? Transaction IDs are very useful for several reasons: Tracking payments – You can search for a specific payment within the application, statements, and/or bank records based upon the Transaction ID; Finding out if a payment was Successful, pending or Failed – banks and applications use the id to determine the current status of a payment; Customer service – When you contact your bank or payment application regarding some issue you may be asked for the Transaction ID; Resolving disputes – Transaction IDs are used to investigate cases of fraudulent activity, charge backs and unauthorized withdrawals; Record keeping – Transaction IDs provide business customers with a method of reconciling payments and matching them to receipts/invoices. Simply put, a Transaction ID is not just another random number. It serves as the primary reference point for all aspects related to the completed transaction. How Does a Transaction ID Work? Every time you initiate a digital payment, multiple systems work together behind the scenes to process the transaction securely. During this process, a unique Transaction ID is generated to identify that specific payment. Here’s a simplified payment workflow: Payment Workflow Payment Workflow Customer Initiates Payment ▼ Bank / UPI App Receives Request ▼ Transaction ID is Generated ▼ Payment is Processed ▼ Bank & Merchant Record the Transaction ▼ Transaction Status Updated (Successful / Pending / Failed) The Transaction ID remains associated with that payment throughout its lifecycle. Whether you’re checking the payment status, requesting a refund, or contacting customer support weeks later, this unique identifier helps locate the transaction instantly. What Does a Transaction ID Look Like? The format of a Transaction ID varies depending on the payment method, bank, or payment service provider. In most cases, it may contain: Numbers only Letters and numbers (alphanumeric) Between 12 and 35 characters , depending on the platform For example: Payment Method Example (Illustrative) UPI 432198765432 Card Payment TXN84A9D271C5 Net Banking NBX47291836452 Payment Gateway CFP9A72X3815Q Note: The examples above are for illustration only. Actual Transaction ID formats vary across banks, payment gateways, and payment apps. Transaction ID vs UTR vs UPI Reference Number One of the most common questions users have is whether a Transaction ID, UTR, and UPI Reference Number are the same. While these terms are often used interchangeably, they refer to slightly different identifiers depending on the payment method and the platform you’re using. Here’s a quick comparison: Feature Transaction ID UTR (Unique Transaction Reference) UPI Reference Number Used for All digital payment types Primarily NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, and bank records UPI payments Generated by Payment app, gateway, or bank Banking system UPI ecosystem Purpose Identify and track a payment Bank-side transaction tracking Identify a specific UPI transaction Where you’ll find it Payment apps, merchant receipts, bank statements Bank statements and transaction history Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, BHIM, and banking apps What is a UPI Transaction ID? A UPI Transaction ID is a unique reference number generated every time you send or receive money using the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) . It serves as proof that a transaction was initiated and allows both users and banks to track its progress. Whether you’re paying a merchant, splitting a restaurant bill with friends, or transferring money between bank accounts, each UPI payment gets its own unique Transaction ID. A UPI Transaction ID can help you: Check whether a payment was successful, pending, or failed. Verify that money has been credited to the recipient. Locate a payment in your transaction history. Raise complaints with your bank or UPI app. Track refunds or payment reversals. Depending on the app you use, the identifier may appear as: UPI Transaction ID UPI Reference Number UPI Ref No. Transaction ID Txn ID Although the label may differ, they all serve the same purpose – identifying a specific UPI payment. How to Find Your UPI Transaction ID Finding your Transaction ID is simple and only takes a few taps. Most UPI apps display it within your payment history. In Google Pay App Open Google Pay . Tap Activity . Select the payment you want to view. Scroll down to find the UPI Transaction ID or Reference Number . In PhonePe App Open PhonePe . Go to History . Select the relevant transaction. The Transaction ID or Reference Number will be displayed in the transaction details. In Paytm App Open Paytm . Navigate to Balance & History or Passbook . Tap the transaction. View the Transaction ID under the payment details. In BHIM UPI App Open the BHIM app. Tap Transactions . Select the payment. The UPI Reference Number will be shown on the transaction details screen. In Bank Mobile Apps or Net Banking You can also locate your Transaction ID through your bank. Log in to your mobile banking app or internet banking portal. Open Transaction History or Account Statement. Find the relevant payment. The Transaction ID, Reference Number, or UTR will be displayed alongside the transaction details. Tip: If you’re contacting customer support about a payment issue, keep your Transaction ID, transaction amount, date, and recipient details handy. This helps the support team locate your payment more quickly. How to Perform a UPI Transaction ID Check A UPI Transaction ID check helps you verify the current status of a payment. This is particularly useful if money has been debited from your account but the recipient hasn’t received it yet. You can check the payment status by: Opening your UPI app and viewing the transaction details. Checking your bank’s transaction history. Contacting your bank or payment app’s customer support and sharing the Transaction ID. Using the Transaction ID to confirm payment with the merchant. Most payment apps display one of the following statuses: Status Meaning Successful The payment has been completed successfully. Pending The payment is still being processed. Failed The transaction could not be completed. Reversed The deducted amount has been returned to your account. Refunded The merchant has initiated a refund. If your payment remains pending for an extended period, avoid making another payment immediately. Instead, check the transaction status first or contact your bank with the Transaction ID. Common Payment Issues and How a Transaction ID Helps Payment issues can happen for several reasons, including network interruptions, banking delays, or temporary server issues. A Transaction ID makes it much easier to identify and resolve these problems. Money Debited but Recipient Didn’t Receive It : This is one of the most common UPI issues. The Transaction ID helps the bank determine whether the payment is still processing, has failed, or has already been reversed. Payment Marked as Pending : Sometimes banks require additional time to complete processing. Instead of initiating another payment, use the Transaction ID to check the payment status or contact customer support. Merchant Can’t Find Your Payment : If you’ve completed a payment but the merchant hasn’t received confirmation, sharing the Transaction ID allows them to locate the transaction in their payment dashboard or with their payment service provider. Need a Refund : Whether it’s a cancelled order or a duplicate payment, the Transaction ID helps businesses trace the original transaction and process refunds more efficiently. Payment Dispute : If you believe you’ve been charged incorrectly or need to raise a complaint, the Transaction ID serves as the primary reference for banks and payment service providers during their investigation. Why Transaction IDs Matter for Businesses For businesses that process hundreds or even thousands of digital payments every day, a Transaction ID is much more than a payment reference – it’s the foundation of efficient payment operations. Every transaction generates a unique identifier that businesses can use to track payments throughout their lifecycle, from authorization and settlement to refunds and reconciliation. Here are some of the key business use cases: Match payments to their orders and invoices. Resolve consumer disputes related to non-receipt of goods/services or duplicated/double charged amounts. Handle refunds and chargebacks. Detect and analyze fraudulent activities. Maintain clean financial records for accounting purposes. The majority of Payment Gateway Dashboards and Reconciliation Tools utilize transaction IDs to maintain alignment among all their systems. Best Practices for Using Transaction IDs Whether you’re an individual or a business, following a few simple practices can make payment tracking much easier. Save the Transaction ID for important or high-value payments. Verify the transaction status before making a duplicate payment. Share the Transaction ID – not sensitive information like your PIN or OTP, when contacting customer support. Keep payment confirmation emails or SMS alerts until the transaction is successfully completed. Businesses should regularly reconcile Transaction IDs with orders, invoices, and settlement reports. These habits can help resolve payment issues more quickly and improve financial record-keeping. Simplify Payment Tracking with Cashfree Payments As your business grows, manually tracking payments across multiple channels can become time-consuming. A reliable payment gateway gives you complete visibility into every transaction, helping you reconcile payments faster, manage refunds efficiently, and resolve customer queries with ease. With Cashfree Payments , you can: Accept payments through UPI, cards, net banking, wallets, and more. Track every transaction in real time from a unified dashboard. Automate payment reconciliation with detailed settlement reports . Process refunds quickly and monitor their status. Reduce operational effort with comprehensive payment insights. Explore Cashfree Payments to streamline payment tracking and simplify your payment operations. Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is a Transaction ID? A Transaction ID is a unique reference number generated for every digital payment. It helps banks, payment apps, merchants, and customers identify, track, and verify a specific transaction. 2. Is a Transaction ID the same as a UPI Transaction ID? A UPI Transaction ID is a type of Transaction ID generated specifically for UPI payments. Depending on the app or bank, it may also be displayed as a UPI Reference Number or Txn ID. 3. How can I perform a UPI Transaction ID check? Open your UPI app, go to your transaction history, and select the relevant payment. The transaction details page will display both the Transaction ID and the current payment status. If you’re unable to verify the payment, you can share the Transaction ID with your bank or payment app’s customer support for assistance. 4. Can I check whether a payment was successful using a Transaction ID? Yes. Banks, UPI apps, and payment service providers use the Transaction ID to verify whether a transaction is successful, pending, failed, refunded, or reversed. 5. Where can I find my Transaction ID? You can find your Transaction ID in the transaction history of your UPI app, bank mobile app, internet banking portal, payment confirmation email, or SMS alert. 6. Is a Transaction ID the same as a UTR? Not always. A Transaction ID is a general identifier for digital payments, while a UTR (Unique Transaction Reference) is commonly used by banks for NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, and some UPI transactions. The terminology may vary depending on your bank or payment platform. 7. Can two transactions have the same Transaction ID? No. Every payment is assigned a unique Transaction ID, ensuring that each transaction can be individually tracked and identified. 8. Can I reverse a payment using the Transaction ID? No. A Transaction ID helps identify and track a payment but does not allow you to reverse it. Refunds and reversals depend on the payment status and the policies of your bank or merchant. 9. What should I do if I can’t find my Transaction ID? Check your transaction history, account statement, payment confirmation email, or SMS alerts. If you still can’t locate it, contact your bank or payment app’s customer support and provide details such as the transaction amount, date, time, and recipient. 10. Why do businesses use Transaction IDs? Businesses use Transaction IDs to reconcile payments, track settlements, process refunds, investigate disputes, detect fraud, and maintain accurate financial records.

title: How Do You Handle AI-Generated Misinformation, Hallucinations, or Inaccurate Brand Mentions?
summary: The ugly truth: brands rarely control their own AI narrative. Here's what to do about it.
body_text: Key Takeaways Brands rarely control their own AI narrative: 84% of AI responses do not cite a brand's own domain at all, meaning most of what AI models say about a company comes from external sources like community platforms, review sites, and news coverage. AI models pull from a wide and varied range of sites per response, from 5.8 domains for Gemini up to 27 for Grok, which is why inconsistent or outdated brand descriptions surface more often in AI search than in traditional search. The fastest way to correct an inaccurate AI-generated description is not to dispute the AI's output directly, but to increase the volume, freshness, and citability of accurate brand information on external sites, paired with structured, schema-marked content. Domain citation rates climbed 8 points quarter over quarter, suggesting that brands actively publishing structured, up-to-date content are already closing the accuracy gap. Misinformation monitoring should be treated as an ongoing discipline rather than a one-time fire drill, since source rankings and model behavior are volatile enough that factual errors can persist in AI answers unnoticed without active, cross-model tracking. Here’s the thing about AI search: answer engines can make mistakes, and it’s critical for marketers to keep on top of brand perception and product descriptions to ensure accuracy. How? By working with LLMs, not against them. So basically, knowing how they operate. We created the State of AI Search 2026 Report to help marketers do just that, specifically by sharing trends we’ve observed from millions of data points spanning 8+ LLMs, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity. However, we also wanted to go deeper and contextualize our findings, turning to extensive conversations with marketers grappling with a whole new acquisition channel that forms its own opinions on which brands or products to recommend. Today, we’re exploring one of the most pressing questions around AI-generated misinformation. Methodology Between December 2025 and March 2026, we collected and analyzed millions of AI-generated responses across B2B and B2C. We also layered the product data with a supplementary analysis of over 500 conversations in Q2 (April-June 2026), including enterprise demos, strategy sessions, and onboarding calls. We identified the most common questions and unresolved priorities for marketing teams building out GEO programs. These companies include both enterprise and mid-market teams, with a median average revenue of $933 million and median average size of 755 employees. Each question in this blog series is answered with benchmark metrics compiled from our product data, along with a series of recommended action items to improve your GEO efforts. You can view the full report here. How Do You Handle AI-Generated Misinformation, Hallucinations, or Inaccurate Brand Mentions? The starting point for any misinformation strategy is understanding how rarely brands actually control the narrative in the first place. Our data shows that 84% of AI responses do not cite a brand's own domain at all , meaning the majority of what AI models say about any given company is synthesized from external sources like community platforms, review sites, competitor comparison pages, and news coverage. Combine that with the fact that AI models pull from a wide and varied range of sites per response (from 5.8 domains for Gemini up to 27 for Grok) and it becomes clear why inconsistent or outdated brand descriptions show up more often in AI search than traditional search, where your website could at least compete directly for the top organic position. Because models are often citing external sources, the fastest way to correct an inaccurate or outdated description is not to dispute the AI's output directly, but increase the volume, freshness, and citability of accurate information about your brand on other sites . This typically involves partnerships to secure high-authority, off-page brand placements, combined with your own structured, schema-marked content to reinforce the correct narrative. The data shows citation rates climbed 8 points quarter over quarter, which suggests that brands actively publishing structured, up-to-date content are already closing this gap. It is also worth treating this as a monitoring discipline, not a one-time fire drill. Because source rankings and model behavior are volatile, a factual error or outdated claim about pricing, leadership, or product capabilities can persist in AI answers before a brand notices, unless it is actively tracked across models on an ongoing basis. Action Items Run a standing audit of what AI models currently say about your brand, pricing, leadership, and core product claims across all seven major models, since inaccuracies often vary by model. When you find an inaccurate or outdated claim, prioritize publishing a clear, structured, schema-marked correction on your own domain and on the specific external source where the error originated, rather than attempting to contest the AI output directly. Keep pricing, leadership, product, and comparison pages current on a defined cadence. Stale on-page information is one of the most common root causes of outdated AI-generated claims. Treat your Domain Citation rate as an early-warning metric. A brand with a very low citation rate has effectively ceded the narrative to other sites, which raises the odds of inaccurate or incomplete descriptions surfacing in AI answers. For more insights, check out the full State of AI Search 2026 report . FAQs How do you handle AI-generated misinformation, hallucinations, or inaccurate brand mentions? The starting point is understanding that brands rarely control their own narrative in AI search, since 84% of AI responses don't cite a brand's own domain at all. Because of this, the most effective correction strategy is not disputing the AI's output directly, but increasing the volume, freshness, and citability of accurate information on external sites, combined with structured, schema-marked content on the brand's own domain, and treating this as an ongoing monitoring discipline rather than a one-time fix. Why do AI models get brand information wrong more often than traditional search? AI models synthesize answers from a wide and varied range of external sources per response, from 5.8 domains for Gemini up to 27 for Grok, rather than pulling primarily from a brand's own website. In traditional search, a brand's website can compete directly for the top organic position, but in AI search, most of what gets said about a company comes from community platforms, review sites, competitor comparisons, and news coverage instead. Why doesn't disputing an AI's incorrect output work as a correction strategy? Since AI models are usually synthesizing external sources rather than a brand's own domain, disputing the model's output directly doesn't address the root cause. Correction is far more effective when brands increase the volume, freshness, and citability of accurate information across the specific external sources the model is drawing from, alongside structured content on their own site. How should marketers correct an inaccurate or outdated AI-generated claim? When an inaccurate or outdated claim is found, the priority is publishing a clear, structured, schema-marked correction both on the brand's own domain and on the specific external source where the error originated, rather than attempting to contest the AI's output directly. What is Domain Citation rate and why does it matter? Domain Citation rate measures how often AI responses actually cite a brand's own domain versus relying on external sources. It functions as an early-warning metric: a brand with a very low citation rate has effectively ceded its narrative to other sites, which raises the odds of inaccurate or incomplete descriptions surfacing in AI-generated answers. Is AI-generated misinformation about brands improving or getting worse? The data shows some improvement, with domain citation rates climbing 8 points quarter over quarter. This suggests that brands actively publishing structured, up-to-date content are already making progress in closing the accuracy gap, though the underlying volatility of AI model behavior means ongoing monitoring is still necessary. How often should brands audit what AI models say about them? Brands should run a standing audit, not a one-time check, of what AI models say about their pricing, leadership, and core product claims across all seven major models, since inaccuracies often vary by model. Pricing, leadership, product, and comparison pages should also be kept current on a defined cadence, since stale on-page information is one of the most common root causes of outdated AI-generated claims.

title: Best AI Video Generators [2026]
summary: AI video generator covers four different technologies. What each costs per finished minute, what the free tiers really give you, and how to pick.
body_text: AI video generator is one phrase covering four different technologies, and picking the wrong category costs far more than picking the wrong brand. Avatar tools turn a script into a synthetic presenter. Generative video models turn a prompt into footage that never existed. Assembly tools cut existing material into something watchable. Explainer tools turn a question into a narrated walkthrough. Almost every roundup on this keyword mixes all four into one ranked list, which is why so many people buy a subscription and then find it does not do the thing they wanted. This guide maps the four categories, names the tools leading each one, and puts verified 2026 prices against them, including what a finished minute of video actually costs. What Does "AI Video Generator" Actually Mean? An AI video generator is any tool that produces video from a non-video input, which in practice covers four unrelated technologies with different inputs, costs, and failure modes. The categories, in the order most people meet them: Avatar video. You write a script, a synthetic presenter delivers it on camera. Built for corporate training, product explainers, and translating one video into thirty languages. Synthesia and HeyGen lead here. Generative video models. You write a prompt, the model invents footage frame by frame. Built for creative, cinematic, and effects work where the shot cannot be filmed. Runway, Google Flow, and Pika lead here. Assembly tools. You supply a recording, a stock library, or an article, and the tool cuts it into something watchable. Built for podcasts, social clips, and repurposing. Descript, InVideo, and Pictory lead here. Explainer video. You ask a question, you get a narrated walkthrough of the answer. Built for onboarding, documentation, and study, where the point is that someone understands the subject afterwards. The fourth category is the one roundups leave out, and its absence is not a ranking judgment. It is a difference of input. The other three all start from material you already have or already imagined. This one starts from something you do not know yet. If you cannot say which of the four you need, no amount of tool comparison will help you. The category is the decision. The brand is a detail. The 2026 AI Video Generator Comparison Table Pricing checked against each vendor's own plan page in August 2026. This category changes monthly, so confirm before you commit. Tool Category Input Best for Pricing model Free tier Synthesia Avatar Script Training, localisation Monthly, minute quota 10 min a month, no download HeyGen Avatar Script or photo Social video, dubbing Monthly, credits 3 videos a month, 1 min, watermarked Runway Generative model Prompt or image Cinematic and effects shots Monthly, credits 125 one time credits Google Flow Generative model Prompt or reference Veo 3.1 clips with native audio Bundled into Google AI plans 50 credits a day Pika Generative model Image or prompt Cheap experimentation Monthly, credits 80 credits a month, 480p Descript Assembly Recording or footage Podcasts, screen recordings Monthly, media hours 60 media minutes, 720p InVideo Assembly Brief or footage Social cuts from a brief Monthly, credits None Pictory Assembly Article or footage Turning long text into video Monthly, credits Trial only, 3 projects Scrimba Explain Explainer A question Understanding a subject Free during open beta Free during open beta Avatar Video: Synthesia and HeyGen Avatar video is the most commercially mature corner of the category, because the job is narrow: read this script convincingly, on camera, in any language. Synthesia prices by minutes of generated video. Its plan page lists a free tier at 10 minutes a month, Starter at $19 a month billed monthly, and Creator at $89 a month or $804 a year for 30 minutes a month. Enterprise removes the minute cap. Note what the free tier withholds: downloading your videos and removing the Synthesia logo both start at Starter, so the free plan makes video you can watch but cannot export. HeyGen prices by credits instead. Its plan page lists a free tier of three videos a month capped at one minute each, Creator at $29 a month with 600 credits and watermark removal, and Pro at $49 a month with 1,000 credits and 4K export. Length and resolution are gated alongside volume, so the tier decides what you can make as well as how much. Both share a quality ceiling. A synthetic presenter reading a script to camera is convincing. The same presenter demonstrating a physical action or carrying real emotional range is not. Avatar tools are excellent at talking head video and nothing else, which is fine, because talking head video is most of corporate video. Generative Video Models: Runway, Google Flow, and Pika Generative video models produce footage that never existed, frame by frame, from a text prompt or a reference image. OpenAI has discontinued Sora. According to OpenAI's help centre , the web and app experiences shut down on 26 April 2026, the API follows on 24 September 2026, and user data is permanently deleted once the export window closes. The best known name in generative video is gone, and anyone who stored work there has a deadline. The most famous tool in a category is not automatically a safe place to keep your work. Runway publishes exact credit costs, which makes it the easiest tool here to reason about. Its pricing page puts Gen-4.5 at 60 credits per five seconds. Standard is $15 a month, or $12 billed yearly for 7,500 credits a year. Pro is $35 a month, or $28 yearly for 27,000 credits. Max is $95 a month, or $76 yearly for 114,000 credits. The free tier is 125 one time credits, and watermark removal starts at Standard. Google Flow is not sold on its own. It is the studio wrapping Veo 3.1, Gemini Omni, and Nano Banana, and access is bundled into Google AI plans at $4.99, $19.99, or from $99.99 a month. Google's support page puts non subscribers at 50 Flow credits a day, AI Plus at 200 a month, AI Pro at 1,000 a month, and AI Ultra at 10,000 or 25,000. A Veo generation costs roughly 10 credits in Lite mode, 20 in Fast, and 100 in Quality, so $19.99 a month buys about ten Quality generations. Pika is the cheapest way in. Its pricing page lists a free tier of 80 credits a month restricted to 480p and image to video, with Standard at $8 a month billed yearly. Unusually, commercial use and watermark free downloads are both included on that free tier, which is not true of most free plans in this article. Every model in this category shares the same limits: Output is measured in seconds. Long form means stitching many short generations together. Physics, hands, and text inside the frame still fail regularly. Continuity across shots is unreliable, so the same character rarely survives three cuts unchanged. Your hit rate is not 100 percent. Most generations get discarded, and every discarded one was paid for. That last point puts real money behind prompt quality, which makes prompt engineering a practical skill here rather than a novelty. Assembly Tools: Descript, InVideo, and Pictory Assembly tools do not invent footage. They cut it. That single difference changes the economics completely, because processing an hour of existing video costs a fraction of generating ten seconds of new video. Descript treats video as a text document: edit the transcript, the video edits itself. Its pricing page lists a free tier at 60 media minutes a month and 720p export, Hobbyist at $16 a month billed yearly for 10 media hours and watermark free 1080p, and Creator at $24 a month yearly for 30 media hours and 4K. InVideo has no free plan at all. Its pricing page starts at Plus, $17 a month or $200 yearly for 75 credits a month, and every paid tier exports without a watermark. Pictory turns long text into video, and its plan structure shows the split between the two kinds of work. According to its pricing page , Starter costs $25 a month billed annually and includes 2,400 minutes of media a year alongside 1,200 AI credits a year. Those credits are worth about 12.5 minutes of generated video. One product, two resources, and the generated one is roughly two hundred times scarcer. Explainer Video: The Category Roundups Leave Out Explainer video starts from a question rather than a script or a prompt, and returns a narrated walkthrough of the answer instead of a produced clip. This is a different product shape. The other three categories assume you already know what the video should say, and the tool's job is production. Here the tool's job is the explanation itself, and the video is how the explanation gets delivered. The use cases are onboarding, documentation, and studying, where the measure of success is that someone understood something. Scrimba Explain sits in this category. It works as an MCP plugin: you ask your coding agent a question, the agent researches it against the files and conversation it already has, and Explain turns the answer into a narrated video walkthrough. It runs with Claude Code, Codex, or any agent supporting MCP , and it works beyond code, with its FAQ naming biology, mathematics, philosophy, and language learning. It is free during open beta. What it is not: no avatars, no stock footage, no brand templates, so it is not an alternative to Synthesia or HeyGen for marketing video. And like any AI tool it can get things wrong, so anything that matters should be double-checked. What a Finished Minute Actually Costs Cost per finished minute is the number the marketing never shows, and it varies by more than an order of magnitude across the four categories. Category Example plan List price What it buys Cost per finished minute Generative model Runway Standard, yearly $144 a year 125 clips of 5 seconds, about 10 minutes About $14 Generative model Runway Max, yearly $912 a year 1,900 clips of 5 seconds, about 158 minutes About $6 Avatar Synthesia Creator $89 a month 30 minutes of avatar video About $3 Assembly Descript Creator, yearly $24 a month 30 media hours a month Fractions of a cent Every figure above is a floor, because each assumes every generation is usable. Nobody's hit rate is that good. For generative model work, double or triple them. Generation speed follows the same pattern, and the vendors say so through their pricing. Pika sells fast , faster , and fastest generation as ascending tiers. HeyGen sells standard, fast, and faster processing the same way. When speed is a paid upgrade across an entire category, the free tier queues by design. Watermarks, Rights, and the Rest of the Fine Print Three constraints decide whether a tool survives a real workflow, and none of them lead the marketing page. Export rights. Most entry paid tiers exist mainly to remove a watermark. Synthesia goes further and gates the download itself. Commercial use. Not uniform. Pika grants it on the free tier while others restrict resolution or volume, and stock library licensing is separate again. Read the plan before building a business process on a free account. Platform risk. Sora's shutdown is the reference case. Keep local copies of anything you would be unhappy to lose, and prefer tools that let you export at full quality on the plan you actually pay for. Which AI Video Generator Do You Actually Need? Pick the category first, then the tool. Match your input to one of these five cases: A person on screen saying your words, in several languages, without filming. Avatar video. HeyGen for a low commitment monthly plan, Synthesia if you need minute quotas and enterprise controls. Footage that does not exist and cannot be filmed. A generative video model. Start with Pika to learn what prompts work at low cost, then move to Runway or Google Flow when quality matters. Budget for discarded takes. A recording, footage, or an article that needs to become a watchable cut. An assembly tool. Descript for anything with a spoken track, InVideo for social output, Pictory for long text. Someone needs to understand something. Explainer video, the category to reach for when the deliverable is comprehension rather than a produced asset. You are not sure yet. Take the free tier in the right category over the best reviewed tool in the wrong one. A limited free plan doing the correct job teaches you more in an afternoon than a month of the wrong subscription. For developers weighing where AI earns its place in a workflow, Scrimba's guide to how web developers can use AI and its roundup of AI tools and courses for learning to code cover the adjacent ground. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best AI video generator in 2026? There is no single best one, because the term covers four different technologies. Synthesia and HeyGen lead avatar video, Runway and Google Flow lead generative video models, Descript leads assembly and editing, and explainer tools handle question to video. Identify your category first, then compare within it. Is there a genuinely free AI video generator? Yes, with real limits. Pika's free tier includes 80 credits a month, commercial use, and no watermark, capped at 480p. Google Flow gives non subscribers 50 credits a day. Descript allows 60 media minutes a month at 720p. Synthesia's free plan cannot download videos at all. What happened to Sora? OpenAI discontinued Sora. The web and app experiences shut down on 26 April 2026, and the API is scheduled to shut down on 24 September 2026. User data is permanently deleted after the final export window closes. Anyone who created work in Sora should export it before the API deadline. How much does AI video cost per minute? It depends entirely on category. At list prices, generative model output runs roughly $6 to $14 per finished minute, avatar video around $3 per minute, and assembly tools a fraction of a cent because they bill media hours rather than generated seconds. Treat all of these as floors, since unusable takes still cost credits. Can I use AI generated video commercially? Sometimes on free tiers and usually on paid ones, but the terms differ per vendor. Pika includes commercial use on its free plan. Other tools restrict resolution, watermarks, or export volume instead. Always read the specific plan page, because commercial rights and stock library licensing are handled separately. Key Takeaways AI video generator describes four distinct technologies: avatar video, generative video models, assembly tools, and explainer video. Choosing the wrong category is the expensive mistake. OpenAI discontinued Sora, with the app gone on 26 April 2026 and the API ending 24 September 2026, which makes export policy a real selection criterion. Generative video runs roughly $6 to $14 per finished minute at list price before discarded takes, while assembly tools cost fractions of a cent per minute. Free tiers are not equivalent. Pika grants commercial use and no watermark, while Synthesia's free plan does not allow downloading video at all.
